questions.s: A 72-year-old man from Gilgit with chronic constipation has 2 days of gross abdominal distension, colicky pain and absolute constipation. He is not peritonitic and observations are stable. Abdominal radiograph shows a large inverted U-shaped loop arising from the pelvis. What is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Emergency laparotomy with sigmoid colectomy and end colostomy
Flexible sigmoidoscopy with insertion of a flatus tube
Barium enema to confirm the diagnosis
questions.e: The 'coffee bean' loop indicates sigmoid volvulus; without peritonitis or signs of ischaemia, it is first decompressed endoscopically with a flatus tube, followed by planned resection because recurrence is common. Laxatives are ineffective and may worsen obstruction.

questions.s: A 68-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation who stopped her anticoagulant has 6 hours of severe central abdominal pain. She is distressed but her abdomen is soft with only mild tenderness. Lactate is 6.2 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Severe pain out of proportion to the signs in a patient with atrial fibrillation, with a high lactate, suggests acute mesenteric ischaemia from an embolus to the superior mesenteric artery; CT angiography confirms it quickly. Plain films are often normal until infarction is advanced.

questions.s: A 26-year-old married woman presents to a THQ emergency room with sudden lower abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain and dizziness. Her last period was 7 weeks ago. BP 88/56 mmHg, pulse 122/min. Which test should be done first?
questions.e: Any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain and shock needs an immediate pregnancy test, as ruptured ectopic pregnancy is the likely cause here; resuscitation and urgent gynaecological surgery follow. Amylase and plain radiographs do not help establish this diagnosis.

questions.s: A 42-year-old woman has 2 days of right upper quadrant pain and fever of 38.4 °C. Murphy's sign is positive, and ultrasound shows gallstones, a thickened gallbladder wall and pericholecystic fluid. Bilirubin is normal. She is fit for surgery. Apart from antibiotics and analgesia, what is the preferred definitive management?
o: Interval cholecystectomy after 3 months, once inflammation has settled
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the same admission
questions.e: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy, within about a week of presentation, is preferred for acute cholecystitis in a fit patient: it shortens hospital stay and avoids recurrent attacks while waiting. ERCP is for stones in the common bile duct, which a normal bilirubin makes unlikely.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man who had an open appendicectomy years ago has colicky central abdominal pain, bilious vomiting and distension for 24 hours. He is afebrile with a soft abdomen, no localised tenderness, and normal lactate and WBC. Radiograph shows dilated small-bowel loops. No hernia is present. What is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Adhesive small-bowel obstruction without signs of strangulation (fever, constant pain, tenderness, raised lactate or WBC) is first managed conservatively with nasogastric decompression, fluids and electrolyte correction, often with a water-soluble contrast study. Laxatives are inappropriate in mechanical obstruction.

questions.s: A 17-year-old boy from Hyderabad has had high fever for 3 weeks, partly treated with antibiotics; blood culture grew Salmonella Typhi resistant to ceftriaxone. He now has sudden worsening abdominal pain with peritonitis and free gas under the diaphragm. Which is the most likely site of perforation?
questions.e: Typhoid perforation occurs typically in the third week at the antimesenteric border of the terminal ileum, where Peyer's patches ulcerate; it requires laparotomy with appropriate antibiotics for XDR typhoid. A perforated duodenal ulcer is commoner overall but does not follow enteric fever.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man has a blast injury to his thigh in a market explosion, with pulsatile bleeding from a deep wound. Firm direct pressure for several minutes has not controlled it. What is the most appropriate next step in the emergency room?
o: Apply a tourniquet proximal to the wound
questions.e: Life-threatening limb haemorrhage that does not stop with direct pressure is controlled with a tourniquet applied proximal to the wound, with the time recorded. Tranexamic acid helps clotting but cannot control arterial bleeding by itself.

questions.s: During a laparotomy for multiple gunshot wounds, a 28-year-old man has received 14 units of blood. His core temperature is 34 °C, pH 7.08 and he oozes from all raw surfaces. The bowel has several perforations and the liver is bleeding. What is the most appropriate surgical strategy?
o: Complete definitive repair now, with bowel anastomoses and liver resection
Damage control: pack, control contamination, temporary closure, ICU
Close the abdomen primarily and transfer to another hospital
Stop operating and give recombinant factor VIIa alone
questions.e: Hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy form the lethal triad; damage control surgery limits the operation to stopping bleeding and contamination, then restores physiology in ICU before definitive repair in a planned return. Prolonged definitive surgery in this state is often fatal.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man with a GCS of 11 after a fall has noisy breathing from his tongue falling back. He gags when an oropharyngeal airway is tried. There is no facial or skull base injury. Which airway adjunct is most appropriate?
questions.e: A nasopharyngeal airway is better tolerated than an oropharyngeal airway in a semi-conscious patient with an intact gag reflex, and is safe when there is no suspected basal skull fracture. A laryngeal mask is not tolerated by a patient with a gag reflex, and a surgical airway is not indicated.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man was standing close to a bomb blast in a crowded market. He has ruptured tympanic membranes, cough with blood-stained sputum and increasing breathlessness; there are no penetrating chest wounds. Chest radiograph shows bilateral perihilar 'butterfly' opacities. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: The pressure wave of an explosion damages air-filled organs; tympanic rupture marks significant exposure, and blast lung presents with haemoptysis, hypoxia and bilateral butterfly opacities. Patients may deteriorate over hours and need careful fluid use and ventilatory support.

questions.s: After a road traffic accident, a man's eyes do not open to any stimulus, he makes only incomprehensible sounds, and his arms and legs extend to a painful stimulus. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale score?
questions.e: No eye opening scores 1, incomprehensible sounds score 2 and extension to pain scores 2, giving 5. Extension (decerebrate posturing) scores 2 and abnormal flexion (decorticate) scores 3.

questions.s: A 22-year-old man was hit with a cricket bat. He talked normally on arrival, but over two hours his GCS falls from 15 to 9 with a dilated left pupil. CT shows a large left biconvex hyperdense collection with midline shift. A neurosurgeon is available. What is the definitive management?
o: Burr hole in the emergency room
Urgent craniotomy and evacuation of the haematoma
Intravenous mannitol and repeat CT in 6 hours
Admission to ICU for intracranial pressure monitoring
questions.e: A large extradural haematoma with deteriorating GCS and a dilated pupil requires urgent craniotomy and evacuation; outcome is excellent if it is done before brainstem compression is established. Mannitol only buys time and should not delay surgery.

questions.s: A 33-year-old man has clear, watery fluid dripping from one nostril, especially when he leans forward, a week after a frontal head injury. Which test on the fluid best confirms that it is cerebrospinal fluid?
questions.e: Beta-2 transferrin is found in CSF and perilymph but not in nasal secretions, tears or serum, making it a specific test for CSF leak. Glucose dipstick testing is unreliable because nasal mucus and blood contain glucose.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man is brought in after being hit by a car. He has a GCS of 7 with a scalp haematoma but no visible external bleeding. BP 76/40 mmHg, pulse 138/min. What is the most appropriate interpretation of his hypotension?
o: It is due to the head injury and needs mannitol
It is neurogenic shock from brain injury
It is the Cushing response to raised intracranial pressure
It suggests bleeding elsewhere until proven otherwise
questions.e: Isolated head injury rarely causes hypotension in adults except in the terminal stage, so hypotension with tachycardia indicates haemorrhage from the chest, abdomen, pelvis or long bones until proven otherwise. The Cushing response causes hypertension with bradycardia, the opposite of this picture.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man with fractured ribs and a small traumatic pneumothorax on the left is stable on room air. He needs general anaesthesia and positive pressure ventilation for fixation of a femur fracture. What is the most appropriate step regarding the pneumothorax?
o: No action, as it is small
Repeat the chest radiograph after the operation
Aspirate with a needle in theatre if he deteriorates
Insert a chest drain before positive pressure ventilation
questions.e: Positive pressure ventilation can convert a small traumatic pneumothorax into a tension pneumothorax, so a chest drain is placed before general anaesthesia or air transfer. Leaving it to be treated only after deterioration under anaesthesia is unsafe.

questions.s: A 50-year-old driver strikes the steering wheel in a frontal collision. He has anterior chest pain and a sternal fracture on lateral radiograph. BP and pulse are normal. Which investigation should be performed to screen for blunt cardiac injury?
questions.e: Blunt cardiac injury is screened with an ECG and troponin; if both are normal, significant injury is very unlikely. Arrhythmias or ECG changes call for monitoring and echocardiography, but coronary angiography and stress testing are not screening tools.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man is crushed under a collapsing wall. The chest radiograph shows a fracture of the left first rib. Why is this finding particularly important?
o: It often causes a flail chest
It signals high-energy trauma with possible subclavian or plexus injury
It usually causes a large pneumothorax that needs a chest drain at once
questions.e: The first rib is short and well protected, so its fracture implies a large force and should raise suspicion of injury to the subclavian vessels, brachial plexus and other thoracic structures. It is not itself a cause of flail chest and is rarely fixed.

questions.s: A 33-year-old man was in a car crash 6 hours ago. He is stable with mild diffuse abdominal tenderness. CT of the abdomen shows a moderate amount of free fluid in the pelvis but no injury to the liver, spleen or kidneys. What does this finding most strongly suggest?
o: Retroperitoneal haematoma from a renal injury
questions.e: Free intraperitoneal fluid without solid organ injury in a man after blunt trauma suggests bowel or mesenteric injury, which CT may otherwise miss; it calls for laparotomy or laparoscopy, or at least very close re-examination. Small amounts of fluid may be physiological in women, but a moderate amount in a man is not.

questions.s: An 18-year-old boy was discharged after a fall from a tree with left-sided chest bruising and a normal examination. Eight days later he collapses at home with left upper quadrant pain and left shoulder pain, and arrives with BP 80/50 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Delayed rupture of a splenic haematoma
Acute pancreatitis from the earlier trauma
questions.e: A subcapsular splenic haematoma can enlarge and rupture days to weeks after the injury, causing sudden haemorrhagic shock with left upper quadrant and shoulder-tip pain. A perforated ulcer causes peritonitis rather than haemorrhagic shock.

questions.s: A 24-year-old man has a single gunshot wound to the anterior abdomen just above the umbilicus, with no exit wound. He is haemodynamically stable and has mild generalised tenderness. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Abdominal ultrasound and discharge if normal
questions.e: Gunshot wounds that penetrate the anterior abdominal wall cause intraperitoneal injury in the large majority of cases because of the energy transferred, so laparotomy is the standard management, especially with tenderness. Selective observation is mainly used for stab wounds.

questions.s: A 3-year-old girl has scattered patches of scald burns from spilt tea. The doctor wants to estimate the burnt area quickly. Approximately what percentage of body surface area is represented by the area of the child's own palm with fingers?
questions.e: The patient's palm including the fingers is about 1% of total body surface area, at any age, which is useful for scattered burns. The rule of nines must be modified for young children, whose heads are proportionally larger.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman spills hot water on her forearm. The area is red, very painful and has large, thin-walled blisters; the base blanches and refills briskly on pressure. How is this burn best classified, and how is it expected to heal?
o: Full thickness; needs excision and grafting
Deep partial thickness; usually heals with scarring after 3 weeks
Epidermal only; heals in 2-3 days without blistering
Superficial partial thickness; heals in about 2 weeks
questions.e: Painful, blistered skin with brisk capillary refill is a superficial partial-thickness burn; the dermal appendages survive, so it heals from them in about 10-14 days with little scarring. Deep partial-thickness burns are less painful, have sluggish or absent refill and take longer to heal.

questions.s: A 9-month-old boy has episodes of inconsolable crying with drawing up of his legs, vomiting, and a stool with blood and mucus. A sausage-shaped mass is felt in the right upper abdomen. He is not peritonitic and is haemodynamically stable after fluids. What is the most appropriate management after confirming the diagnosis on ultrasound?
o: Observation and repeat ultrasound in 24 hours
Reduction by air enema under imaging
questions.e: Intermittent colic, vomiting, redcurrant-jelly stool and a sausage-shaped mass indicate intussusception; in a stable child without peritonitis or perforation, radiological reduction by air (or contrast) enema is first line. Laparotomy is reserved for failed reduction, peritonitis or perforation.

questions.s: A 68-year-old man with known diverticular disease is septic with generalised peritonitis. At laparotomy there is faecal contamination throughout the abdomen from a perforated sigmoid colon. Which operation is most appropriate?
o: Primary resection and anastomosis without a stoma
Sigmoid resection with end colostomy (Hartmann's procedure)
questions.e: Faecal peritonitis from a perforated sigmoid diverticulum in a septic patient is managed by resecting the diseased segment with an end colostomy and closure of the rectal stump, avoiding an anastomosis in a contaminated field. Lavage alone is not appropriate when there is faecal contamination.

questions.s: Ayesha, a 32-year-old teacher from Hyderabad, has had 18 months of progressive difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids from the start, with regurgitation of undigested food at night and 5 kg weight loss. A barium swallow shows a dilated oesophagus with a smooth, tapered narrowing at the gastro-oesophageal junction. Upper GI endoscopy shows no mucosal lesion. Which investigation best confirms the diagnosis?
questions.e: Dysphagia to solids and liquids from onset with a bird's-beak narrowing suggests achalasia, and manometry confirms it by showing absent peristalsis and failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation. pH monitoring assesses reflux, not motility; CT and endoscopic ultrasound are used when pseudoachalasia from a tumour is suspected, which a normal endoscopy in a young patient makes unlikely.

questions.s: A 65-year-old man from rural Sindh, a lifelong smoker, presents with 3 months of progressive dysphagia, first to solids and now to semi-solids, and has lost 8 kg. Examination shows no lymphadenopathy. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: Contrast-enhanced CT of chest and abdomen
questions.e: Progressive dysphagia with weight loss in an older smoker is oesophageal cancer until proven otherwise, and endoscopy allows direct visualisation and biopsy for a tissue diagnosis. CT and PET-CT are staging tests used after histology is confirmed; a barium swallow shows a stricture but cannot provide tissue.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man vomits forcefully several times after a large meal and alcohol at a party. Shortly afterwards he develops severe retrosternal and upper abdominal pain radiating to the back. He is sweaty, pulse 118/min, and there is crepitus in the neck. Chest X-ray shows pneumomediastinum and a left pleural effusion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Severe chest pain after forceful vomiting with surgical emphysema, pneumomediastinum and a left effusion indicates full-thickness rupture of the distal oesophagus (Boerhaave syndrome). A Mallory-Weiss tear is a mucosal tear that causes haematemesis without mediastinal air; a perforated duodenal ulcer gives free gas under the diaphragm, not in the mediastinum.

questions.s: A 52-year-old man with long-standing heartburn undergoes upper GI endoscopy. Salmon-pink mucosa extends 4 cm above the gastro-oesophageal junction. Biopsies show intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells and no dysplasia. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Endoscopic mucosal resection of the segment
questions.e: Non-dysplastic Barrett's oesophagus is managed with acid suppression and periodic endoscopic surveillance to detect dysplasia early. Ablation and endoscopic resection are reserved for dysplasia or early cancer, and fundoplication controls reflux but does not reverse metaplasia or remove the need for surveillance.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man from a village in Balochistan, who smokes and habitually drinks very hot tea, is found on endoscopy to have an ulcerated stricture in the middle third of the oesophagus. What is the most likely histological type of the tumour?
questions.e: Smoking, very hot beverages and a mid-oesophageal location point to squamous cell carcinoma, the commonest type in South Asia. Adenocarcinoma typically arises in the lower third on a background of Barrett's oesophagus and reflux.

questions.s: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department of a THQ hospital 4 hours after deliberately drinking an acidic toilet cleaner. She is drooling and complains of painful swallowing. Pulse 96/min, BP 120/80 mmHg, abdomen soft and non-tender, and chest X-ray is normal. What is the most appropriate next step after initial stabilisation?
o: Give oral sodium bicarbonate to neutralise
Blind nasogastric tube insertion and lavage
questions.e: In a stable patient without perforation, early endoscopy (within about 24 hours) grades the corrosive injury and guides feeding and follow-up. Inducing vomiting re-exposes the oesophagus, neutralisation causes an exothermic reaction, and blind tube insertion risks perforation.

questions.s: A 72-year-old retired clerk complains of bad breath, regurgitation of undigested food several hours after meals and a gurgling sound in his neck on swallowing. He has had two episodes of aspiration pneumonia. A soft swelling appears on the left side of his neck after eating. What is the safest initial investigation?
questions.e: Delayed regurgitation, halitosis and a gurgling neck swelling suggest a pharyngeal (Zenker's) pouch, best shown by a barium swallow. Blind endoscopy can enter the pouch and perforate it, so it is not the safest first test.

questions.s: A 68-year-old woman has intermittent chest pain and fullness after meals. Barium study shows a large paraoesophageal hiatus hernia with most of the stomach above the diaphragm and the gastro-oesophageal junction in its normal position. Surgical repair is recommended. Which complication is the main reason?
questions.e: In a paraoesophageal (rolling) hernia the stomach can twist and strangulate, so symptomatic hernias are repaired to prevent gastric volvulus. Barrett's change and adenocarcinoma are linked to reflux, which is a feature of sliding rather than paraoesophageal hernias.

questions.s: A 55-year-old woman with achalasia develops severe chest pain, fever and neck crepitus 6 hours after pneumatic dilatation of the oesophagus. Pulse 110/min. Which investigation best confirms the suspected complication?
questions.e: Chest pain, fever and crepitus after dilatation suggest oesophageal perforation, confirmed by a water-soluble contrast swallow (or CT with oral contrast) showing leakage. Barium causes mediastinitis if it leaks, and further endoscopy with insufflation can enlarge the tear.

questions.s: Bilal, a 40-year-old labourer who takes diclofenac regularly for back pain, develops sudden severe epigastric pain that spreads over the whole abdomen. He lies still, and the abdomen is rigid with absent bowel sounds. Pulse 112/min. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Sudden generalised peritonitis in an NSAID user suggests a perforated peptic ulcer, and an erect chest X-ray showing air under the diaphragm is the quick first test. Endoscopy is contraindicated in suspected perforation, and amylase may be mildly raised in perforation so it does not confirm the diagnosis.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man with a long history of untreated peptic ulcer disease has had a week of projectile vomiting of food eaten the previous day. He is dehydrated and a succussion splash is present. Which biochemical pattern is most likely?
o: Hyperchloraemic normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
Hyperkalaemic high anion gap metabolic acidosis
questions.e: Gastric outlet obstruction causes loss of hydrochloric acid in vomitus, giving hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis, with hypokalaemia from renal potassium loss. Acidosis would be expected with diarrhoea or lower intestinal losses, not pure gastric losses.

questions.s: A 46-year-old man with pyloric stenosis from chronic duodenal ulceration has been vomiting for 10 days. Arterial pH is 7.55 and serum potassium 2.6 mmol/L, yet his urine pH is 5.0. Which mechanism best explains the acidic urine?
o: Increased renal ammonia production from hyperchloraemia
Suppressed aldosterone due to the metabolic alkalosis
Aldosterone-driven sodium retention in exchange for H+
questions.e: Volume depletion activates aldosterone, and when potassium is depleted the distal tubule retains sodium by excreting hydrogen ions instead, producing paradoxical aciduria. Aldosterone is raised, not suppressed, and these patients are hypochloraemic, so the other mechanisms do not fit.

questions.s: A 58-year-old man presents with haematemesis and melaena. After resuscitation, endoscopy shows an ulcer on the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum with a visible vessel. Erosion of which artery is most likely responsible for the bleeding?
questions.e: The gastroduodenal artery runs directly behind the first part of the duodenum, so posterior duodenal ulcers erode it and can bleed massively. The left gastric artery is the usual source in lesser-curve gastric ulcers, and the splenic artery is related to posterior gastric ulcers eroding into the pancreas region.

questions.s: A 63-year-old man has 4 months of early satiety, epigastric discomfort and 10 kg weight loss. Hb is 9.1 g/dL. On examination there is a hard, non-tender lymph node in the left supraclavicular fossa behind the clavicular head of sternocleidomastoid. What is this node called?
questions.e: An enlarged left supraclavicular node (Virchow's node, Troisier's sign) reflects lymphatic spread of abdominal malignancy, classically gastric cancer, via the thoracic duct. The Irish node is in the left axilla, a Sister Mary Joseph nodule is umbilical, and the Delphian node is prelaryngeal.

questions.s: A 49-year-old woman with dyspepsia undergoes endoscopy. Gastric biopsy shows low-grade MALT lymphoma confined to the stomach, and Helicobacter pylori is detected. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.e: Most localised low-grade gastric MALT lymphomas associated with H. pylori regress after eradication therapy, so this is first-line. Radiotherapy and chemotherapy are kept for persistent, H. pylori-negative or advanced disease, and gastrectomy is no longer routine.

questions.s: A 45-year-old woman had a partial gastrectomy with gastrojejunostomy 3 months ago. About 20 minutes after meals she gets palpitations, sweating, flushing, abdominal cramps and diarrhoea, and needs to lie down. Blood glucose during an episode is 112 mg/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Symptoms within 30 minutes of eating, caused by rapid entry of hyperosmolar food into the small bowel with fluid shifts, define early dumping. Late dumping occurs 1-3 hours after meals and is due to reactive hypoglycaemia, which a normal glucose here argues against.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man had a total gastrectomy for gastric cancer 3 years ago and has had no follow-up since. He now has tiredness and tingling in his feet. Hb is 8.9 g/dL with MCV 114 fL. What is the most likely cause of his anaemia?
questions.e: Removing the stomach removes parietal cells and intrinsic factor, so B12 cannot be absorbed and stores run out after a few years, causing macrocytic anaemia and neuropathy. Iron deficiency also follows gastrectomy but produces microcytosis, and folate deficiency does not cause neuropathy; lifelong B12 injections are needed.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man has a 5 cm smooth submucosal mass in the body of the stomach found during endoscopy for anaemia. Endoscopic ultrasound-guided biopsy shows spindle cells that stain positive for CD117 (KIT). What is the diagnosis?
questions.e: A spindle-cell submucosal tumour positive for CD117 (KIT) is a gastrointestinal stromal tumour, arising from interstitial cells of Cajal. A leiomyoma is also spindle-celled but is KIT-negative and desmin-positive.

questions.s: A 68-year-old woman is referred for tiredness. Hb is 8.2 g/dL with MCV 68 fL. She has no change in bowel habit and no visible rectal bleeding. Examination reveals a firm, irregular mass in the right iliac fossa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Crohn's disease of the terminal ileum
questions.e: Right-sided colon cancers often present with occult bleeding and iron-deficiency anaemia plus a mass, because the wide lumen and liquid stool delay obstruction. Sigmoid cancers usually cause altered bowel habit and obstruction, and an appendix mass would be accompanied by recent pain and fever.

questions.s: A 62-year-old man presents to a surgical clinic in Lahore with 3 months of looser stools, blood mixed with the stool and 6 kg weight loss. Digital rectal examination is normal. What is the investigation of choice?
questions.e: Colonoscopy visualises the whole colon and allows biopsy for histology, making it the investigation of choice for suspected colorectal cancer. CT colonography is an alternative for frail patients but cannot take tissue, and CEA is used for monitoring, not diagnosis.

questions.s: A 19-year-old man is referred because his father died of colon cancer at 38. Colonoscopy shows several hundred adenomatous polyps throughout the colon and rectum. A germline mutation in which gene is most likely?
questions.e: Hundreds of colorectal adenomas in a young person with early family cancer indicate familial adenomatous polyposis, caused by germline APC mutation on chromosome 5. MLH1 is a mismatch-repair gene in Lynch syndrome, which produces few polyps despite a high cancer risk.

questions.s: A 66-year-old man has 4 days of left iliac fossa pain and fever of 38.6 °C. He is tender in the left iliac fossa without generalised peritonitis. CT shows sigmoid diverticulitis with a 6 cm pericolic abscess and no free gas. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral antibiotics and early outpatient review
questions.e: A large diverticular abscess without generalised peritonitis is treated with IV antibiotics and image-guided percutaneous drainage. Hartmann's procedure is for purulent or faecal peritonitis or failed drainage, and colonoscopy is delayed about 6 weeks because of perforation risk.

questions.s: A 72-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation who stopped her warfarin develops sudden severe central abdominal pain. She is in agony but the abdomen is soft with only mild tenderness. Serum lactate is 6.1 mmol/L (normal < 2). What is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Pain out of proportion to signs with a raised lactate in a patient with atrial fibrillation suggests acute mesenteric embolism, and CT angiography shows the occlusion and bowel viability. A plain X-ray is usually normal early, and colonoscopy does not assess the superior mesenteric artery.

questions.s: A 4-year-old boy is brought with painless passage of a large amount of dark red blood per rectum. He is pale, Hb 7.4 g/dL, and the abdomen is soft and non-tender. Upper GI endoscopy is normal. Which investigation is most likely to identify the cause?
questions.e: Painless heavy rectal bleeding in a young child suggests a Meckel's diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa, which takes up technetium-99m pertechnetate. Barium studies rarely fill the diverticulum, and colonoscopy does not reach the ileum where it lies.

questions.s: A 28-year-old man with known ulcerative colitis is admitted with a severe flare: 10 bloody stools a day, fever 38.8 °C and pulse 120/min. After 72 hours of IV hydrocortisone he is no better, and abdominal X-ray shows the transverse colon dilated to 7 cm. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Continue IV steroids for another week
questions.e: Toxic megacolon failing medical therapy needs urgent subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy, leaving the rectum for later definitive surgery. Prolonging steroids risks perforation, and a restorative pouch is not done in an unwell emergency patient.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman with known Crohn's disease has had four admissions in a year with colicky pain, distension and vomiting despite optimal medical therapy. MR enterography shows a single 10 cm fibrotic stricture of the terminal ileum with upstream dilatation; the rest of the bowel is normal. What is the most appropriate operation?
questions.e: Surgery in Crohn's disease aims to conserve bowel, so a symptomatic terminal ileal stricture is treated by limited resection to macroscopically healthy margins. Wide margins do not reduce recurrence and waste bowel, and bypass leaves diseased bowel in place with a risk of blind-loop problems and cancer.

questions.s: A 26-year-old woman from Peshawar has 4 months of low-grade evening fever, weight loss and colicky right-sided abdominal pain. A doughy mass is felt in the right iliac fossa. Colonoscopy shows transverse ulcers at the ileocaecal valve, and biopsy shows caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli. There is no obstruction. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli confirm ileocaecal tuberculosis, which responds to standard anti-tuberculous therapy; surgery is kept for complications such as obstruction or perforation. Steroids and immunosuppressants for presumed Crohn's disease would worsen tuberculosis, which is why the distinction matters.

questions.s: A 19-year-old student has acute appendicitis. His pain began around the umbilicus before moving to the right iliac fossa. The early periumbilical pain is referred along visceral afferent fibres entering which spinal cord segment?
questions.e: The appendix is a midgut structure, and its visceral afferents enter the cord at about T10, so early pain is felt around the umbilicus (T10 dermatome). Localised right iliac fossa pain comes later, when the inflamed appendix irritates the somatically innervated parietal peritoneum.

questions.s: A 22-year-old man has right iliac fossa pain and fever. When the examiner presses deeply in the left iliac fossa, the patient feels pain in the right iliac fossa. What is this sign called?
questions.e: Pain in the right iliac fossa on pressing the left side is Rovsing's sign, supporting appendicitis. The psoas sign is pain on hip extension (retrocaecal appendix), the obturator sign is pain on internal rotation of the flexed hip (pelvic appendix), and Murphy's sign relates to the gallbladder.

questions.s: Rukhsana, 26 weeks pregnant, has 24 hours of right-sided abdominal pain, nausea and fever of 38 °C. Tenderness is maximal in the right flank, above the usual McBurney's point. WBC is 15,000/mm³. Ultrasound does not visualise the appendix. Which imaging study is most appropriate next?
questions.e: When ultrasound is inconclusive in pregnancy, MRI without contrast is the preferred next test for appendicitis because it is accurate and avoids ionising radiation. CT is accurate but exposes the fetus to radiation, and the pregnant uterus displaces the appendix upwards, explaining the higher tenderness.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man presents 6 days after the onset of right iliac fossa pain. He has a temperature of 37.9 °C and a tender, ill-defined mass in the right iliac fossa without signs of generalised peritonitis. CT shows an inflammatory phlegmon around the appendix with no abscess. What is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: An appendix mass (phlegmon) presenting late is usually managed non-operatively with IV antibiotics and close observation, because early surgery through inflamed, adherent tissue risks bowel injury. Percutaneous drainage is for a drainable abscess, which is absent here.

questions.s: A 22-year-old woman recovers well after an appendicectomy for acute appendicitis. Histology reports a 0.8 cm well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour at the tip of the appendix with clear margins and no mesoappendiceal invasion. What is the most appropriate further management?
questions.e: A small (under 1 cm) appendiceal neuroendocrine tumour at the tip that is completely excised has a very low risk of spread, so appendicectomy alone is curative. Right hemicolectomy is considered for tumours over 2 cm, at the base, or with mesoappendiceal invasion or positive margins.

questions.s: A 9-year-old boy has right iliac fossa pain and fever of 39 °C for 2 days, following a sore throat last week. Tenderness is vague and moves when he turns to his left side, and he has enlarged cervical lymph nodes. Ultrasound shows a normal appendix and several enlarged nodes in the right iliac fossa mesentery. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: High fever, recent upper respiratory infection, shifting tenderness and enlarged mesenteric nodes with a normal appendix suggest mesenteric lymphadenitis, which settles with supportive care. In appendicitis the fever is usually lower and tenderness stays fixed in the right iliac fossa.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man has 18 hours of lower abdominal pain, frequent loose stools and urinary frequency. Abdominal tenderness is mild, but rectal examination is tender on the right, and pain is produced by internally rotating his flexed right hip. Urinalysis shows a few white cells. Where is his inflamed appendix most likely to lie?
questions.e: A pelvic appendix irritates the rectum and bladder, causing diarrhoea, frequency and pyuria, with right-sided rectal tenderness and a positive obturator sign. A retrocaecal appendix gives flank tenderness and a positive psoas sign instead.

questions.s: Five days after appendicectomy for a perforated appendix, a 27-year-old man develops swinging fever, frequent passage of mucus per rectum and lower abdominal discomfort. The wound looks healthy. On rectal examination there is a tender, boggy swelling anteriorly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Swinging fever, mucus diarrhoea and a tender anterior rectal swelling after peritonitis indicate a pelvic abscess, which may drain into the rectum or need image-guided drainage. C. difficile colitis causes watery diarrhoea without a palpable rectal mass, and a subphrenic abscess causes shoulder-tip pain and basal chest signs.

questions.s: During an open appendicectomy through a gridiron incision, the surgeon delivers the caecum but cannot see the appendix. Which landmark most reliably leads to the base of the appendix?
questions.e: The three taeniae coli converge on the base of the appendix, so following them along the caecum always leads to it, whatever the position of the tip. The fold of Treves is on the antimesenteric border of the terminal ileum and does not reliably lead to the base.

questions.s: A 28-year-old woman has had severe pain during and for an hour after defecation for 8 weeks, with streaks of bright red blood on the toilet paper. She is constipated. Gentle parting of the buttocks shows a longitudinal tear in the posterior midline with a sentinel tag. She is already using fibre and laxatives. What is the most appropriate next treatment?
questions.e: A chronic posterior midline fissure is first treated medically with a topical agent such as diltiazem or glyceryl trinitrate to relax the internal sphincter, alongside stool softening. Sphincterotomy is effective but carries a risk of incontinence, so it is kept for failure of medical treatment; anal dilatation is abandoned because of incontinence.

questions.s: A 32-year-old man has a painless anal fissure on the right lateral side, several large oedematous skin tags and an episode of perianal abscess last year. He also reports intermittent diarrhoea and weight loss. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.e: A fissure off the midline, especially if painless and with large tags, suggests an underlying cause such as Crohn's disease, tuberculosis or HIV, and diarrhoea with weight loss strengthens the suspicion. Investigation comes first; sphincterotomy in Crohn's disease risks non-healing wounds and incontinence.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man has 3 days of throbbing perianal pain, worse on sitting, and fever of 38.4 °C. There is a tender, red, fluctuant swelling 3 cm from the anal verge at the 5 o'clock position. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: A fluctuant perianal abscess needs prompt incision and drainage; antibiotics alone do not resolve pus. Searching for and laying open a fistula at the first operation risks creating a false tract or dividing sphincter, so fistula surgery is usually deferred.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man has a chronic discharging opening 2 cm from the anal verge at the 7 o'clock position (patient in lithotomy). He had a drained perianal abscess a year ago. According to Goodsall's rule, where is the internal opening most likely to be?
o: Anterior midline via a straight tract
Directly opposite via a radial tract
Posterior midline via a curved tract
At the dentate line at 9 o'clock
questions.e: Goodsall's rule states that external openings posterior to the transverse anal line usually track in a curved path to an internal opening in the posterior midline. Openings anterior to the line usually track radially in a straight line to the nearest crypt.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man presents 36 hours after the sudden appearance of an exquisitely painful, tense, bluish lump at the anal margin after straining. The lump is covered by skin and is 1.5 cm across. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: An acutely thrombosed external haemorrhoid seen within about 72 hours is best treated by excision or evacuation of the clot under local anaesthesia for rapid pain relief. Banding and sclerotherapy are for internal haemorrhoids above the dentate line; used on skin-covered tissue they cause severe pain.

questions.s: A 45-year-old shopkeeper has bright red blood on the toilet paper and a lump that comes down when he strains and goes back on its own. Proctoscopy shows internal haemorrhoids. Three months of high-fibre diet and fluids have not helped. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Second-degree internal haemorrhoids (prolapsing but reducing spontaneously) that fail conservative measures are treated with rubber band ligation as an outpatient. Excisional haemorrhoidectomy is kept for third- or fourth-degree or recurrent haemorrhoids, and sphincterotomy is a fissure operation.

questions.s: A proctoscopy is performed on a patient in the lithotomy position. At which positions are the primary internal haemorrhoids classically found?
questions.e: Primary internal haemorrhoids lie at 3, 7 and 11 o'clock in the lithotomy position, corresponding to the left lateral, right posterior and right anterior positions of the anal cushions. Midline 6 and 12 o'clock positions are typical of fissures, not haemorrhoids.

questions.s: A 58-year-old woman has a painful bleeding ulcer in the anal canal. Biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma. Staging shows a 4 cm tumour with no distant metastases. What is the first-line treatment?
questions.e: Squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal is treated primarily with chemoradiotherapy, which cures most patients and preserves the sphincter. Abdominoperineal resection is kept for residual or recurrent disease, unlike rectal adenocarcinoma where surgery is the main treatment.

questions.s: A 2-year-old boy from Multan has had several episodes of rectal prolapse that his mother reduces by hand. He is below the 3rd centile for weight, passes bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools and has been treated for pneumonia three times. Which investigation is most likely to reveal the underlying cause?
questions.e: Rectal prolapse with steatorrhoea, failure to thrive and recurrent chest infections suggests cystic fibrosis, confirmed by a sweat chloride test. Malnutrition, diarrhoea and worms are commoner causes of childhood prolapse, but they do not explain the chest infections and greasy stools.

questions.s: A 45-year-old woman has 24 hours of constant right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right shoulder, vomiting and fever of 38.2 °C. She stops breathing in when the examiner presses below the right costal margin. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Fever, right upper quadrant pain and a positive Murphy's sign suggest acute cholecystitis, and ultrasound is the first-line test, showing stones, wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid. HIDA scanning is reserved for doubtful cases, and MRCP is used to look for duct stones.

questions.s: A fit 40-year-old woman is admitted with acute calculous cholecystitis confirmed on ultrasound. Symptoms began 2 days ago and she is improving on IV antibiotics. Liver function tests and the common bile duct are normal. What is the most appropriate surgical plan?
o: Antibiotics alone with no planned surgery
questions.e: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy, within a week of diagnosis, shortens hospital stay and avoids recurrent attacks while waiting, with similar complication rates to delayed surgery. Cholecystostomy is for patients too unwell or frail for surgery, and antibiotics alone leave a high risk of recurrence.

questions.s: A 65-year-old woman has fever with rigors, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. BP 100/60 mmHg after fluids, bilirubin 6.2 mg/dL. Ultrasound shows gallstones and a common bile duct of 11 mm with a stone at its lower end. Blood cultures are taken and IV antibiotics started. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.e: Charcot's triad with a duct stone indicates acute cholangitis, and patients who do not settle promptly or are septic need urgent biliary decompression by ERCP. MRCP adds nothing when ultrasound already shows the stone, and emergency cholecystectomy does not drain the infected duct.

questions.s: A 78-year-old woman has 3 days of colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and distension. She has had previous episodes of right upper quadrant pain. Abdominal X-ray shows dilated small bowel loops, air in the biliary tree and a rounded opacity in the right iliac fossa. She has had no abdominal operations. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Small bowel obstruction, pneumobilia and an ectopic gallstone (Rigler's triad) indicate gallstone ileus, where a large stone enters the bowel through a cholecystoduodenal fistula and impacts near the ileocaecal valve. Adhesions are unlikely without previous surgery and do not cause air in the biliary tree.

questions.s: During a laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the surgeon dissects the hepatocystic (Calot's) triangle to achieve the critical view of safety. Which structure normally lies within this triangle?
questions.e: Calot's triangle is bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the inferior surface of the liver, and contains the cystic artery (usually from the right hepatic artery). The portal vein lies behind the common bile duct in the free edge of the lesser omentum, outside the triangle.

questions.s: Four days after an uneventful laparoscopic cholecystectomy, a 46-year-old woman has mild right upper quadrant pain and her subhepatic drain is producing 400 mL of bile a day. She is afebrile with stable vital signs and no peritonitis. Imaging shows a leak from the cystic duct stump with an intact common bile duct. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Removal of the drain and observation
questions.e: A cystic duct stump leak in a stable patient is managed by ERCP with sphincterotomy and/or a stent, which lowers pressure in the bile duct so bile flows into the duodenum and the leak seals. Relaparotomy is for uncontrolled sepsis, and hepaticojejunostomy is for major transection injuries of the bile duct.

questions.s: A 55-year-old woman has jaundice and recurrent right upper quadrant pain. MRCP shows a large stone impacted in the neck of the gallbladder, compressing and narrowing the common hepatic duct from outside, with dilated intrahepatic ducts. The lower common bile duct is normal calibre and contains no stones. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: External compression of the common hepatic duct by a stone impacted in Hartmann's pouch or the cystic duct is Mirizzi syndrome, and recognising it before cholecystectomy reduces the risk of bile duct injury. In choledocholithiasis the stone lies within the duct itself.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man has an abdominal ultrasound for a kidney problem, which shows several small gallstones in a thin-walled gallbladder. He has never had abdominal pain, and liver function tests are normal. What is the most appropriate advice?
questions.e: Most people with asymptomatic gallstones never develop symptoms, so they are not treated and are told to return if biliary pain develops. Ursodeoxycholic acid is ineffective for most stones and recurrence is common after stopping it.

questions.s: A 42-year-old woman is admitted with mild acute gallstone pancreatitis. By day 4 her pain has settled, she is eating, and liver function tests are returning to normal. Ultrasound showed gallstones and a normal common bile duct. What is the most appropriate plan for her gallbladder?
questions.e: After mild gallstone pancreatitis, cholecystectomy during the same admission (or within about two weeks) prevents recurrent pancreatitis, which is common while waiting. ERCP alone is reserved for patients unfit for surgery.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man from Karachi has 2 weeks of fever, right upper quadrant pain and weight loss. He had bloody diarrhoea a few months ago. There is tender hepatomegaly and intercostal tenderness on the right. Ultrasound shows a single 6 cm hypoechoic lesion in the right lobe, and Entamoeba serology is positive. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
o: Oral metronidazole then a luminal agent
Open surgical drainage of the abscess
questions.e: Most amoebic liver abscesses respond to metronidazole, followed by a luminal amoebicide such as diloxanide to clear gut cysts. Drainage is reserved for failure to respond, very large left-lobe abscesses at risk of rupture into the pericardium, or diagnostic doubt.

questions.s: A 30-year-old shepherd from Balochistan, who keeps dogs to guard his sheep, has a dull ache in the right upper quadrant. Ultrasound shows an 8 cm cyst in the right lobe of the liver containing several smaller cysts within it. Which organism is the most likely cause?
questions.e: A liver cyst with daughter cysts in a person in close contact with sheep and dogs is a hydatid cyst caused by Echinococcus granulosus; humans are accidental intermediate hosts after ingesting eggs from dog faeces. Entamoeba causes a solid-looking abscess without daughter cysts, and Taenia solium causes cysticercosis mainly in muscle and brain.

questions.s: A 34-year-old man is scheduled for surgical removal of an 8 cm hepatic hydatid cyst. To reduce the risk of recurrence from spilled protoscolices, which drug is given before and after the operation?
questions.e: Albendazole is given around surgery or PAIR for hydatid disease to sterilise the cyst and reduce secondary hydatidosis if contents spill. Metronidazole treats amoebic abscess, while ivermectin and diethylcarbamazine are used for other parasites and have no role here.

questions.s: A 62-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes has 10 days of high fever with rigors and right upper quadrant pain. CT shows a 6 cm multiloculated liver abscess. Blood cultures grow Klebsiella pneumoniae. Amoebic serology is negative. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral metronidazole as for amoebic abscess
IV antibiotics alone for 48 hours then home
questions.e: A pyogenic liver abscess of this size needs prolonged antibiotics together with image-guided percutaneous drainage. Metronidazole alone treats amoebic abscess and does not cover Klebsiella, and hepatectomy is reserved for rare cases failing drainage.

questions.s: A 58-year-old man with hepatitis C cirrhosis attends routine surveillance. Ultrasound shows a new 3 cm solid lesion in segment VI, and serum alpha-fetoprotein is raised. Which investigation is most appropriate to establish the diagnosis?
questions.e: In a cirrhotic liver, a lesion over 1 cm showing arterial-phase enhancement with portal venous washout on multiphase CT or MRI is diagnostic of hepatocellular carcinoma without histology. Biopsy is kept for atypical imaging because it risks bleeding and needle-track seeding, and PET is insensitive for HCC.

questions.s: A 52-year-old woman with compensated cirrhosis due to chronic hepatitis B attends a liver clinic in Islamabad. She asks how she will be screened for liver cancer. What is the most appropriate surveillance?
questions.e: Patients with cirrhosis are offered ultrasound about every 6 months, with or without AFP, to detect hepatocellular carcinoma at a treatable stage. AFP alone misses many tumours, and frequent CT adds radiation and cost without clear benefit.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man is brought after a motorbike accident with right upper quadrant pain. After 1 litre of crystalloid his pulse is 88/min and BP 124/78 mmHg, and he stays stable. Contrast CT shows a grade III liver laceration with a small amount of haemoperitoneum and no contrast blush; there are no other injuries. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Selective embolisation of the hepatic artery
questions.e: Haemodynamically stable patients with blunt liver injury, even of high grade, are managed non-operatively with monitoring, serial examination and haemoglobin checks in a unit able to operate. Embolisation is used when CT shows active contrast extravasation, and laparotomy is for instability or peritonitis.

questions.s: During a trauma laparotomy for a bleeding liver laceration, the surgeon clamps the hepatoduodenal ligament (Pringle manoeuvre). Dark blood continues to well up from behind the liver. Which source of bleeding is most likely?
o: Retrohepatic vena cava or hepatic veins
Right branch of the portal vein
questions.e: The Pringle manoeuvre occludes the hepatic artery and portal vein in the free edge of the lesser omentum, so bleeding that continues despite it points to the hepatic veins or retrohepatic vena cava, which drain outside that clamp. Portal and arterial bleeding should stop when the clamp is applied.

questions.s: A 60-year-old woman had an anterior resection for rectal cancer 2 years ago. Her CEA is now rising, and CT and MRI show two metastases confined to the right lobe of the liver, with no disease elsewhere. She is fit, and the remaining liver volume would be adequate. Which treatment gives her the best chance of long-term survival?
questions.e: Resectable colorectal liver metastases without extrahepatic disease can be cured in a meaningful proportion of patients by hepatic resection, usually with perioperative chemotherapy. Transplantation is not standard for colorectal metastases, and whole-liver radiotherapy is palliative.

questions.s: A 38-year-old woman has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting. Serum lipase is five times the upper limit of normal. She does not drink alcohol. Which investigation should be performed early to identify the likely cause?
questions.e: Gallstones are the commonest cause of acute pancreatitis, and early ultrasound detects them and guides decisions about ERCP and cholecystectomy. Contrast CT is not needed when the diagnosis is clear and is best delayed, and endoscopic ultrasound is used later for unexplained cases.

questions.s: A 47-year-old man is admitted with acute pancreatitis. The diagnosis is clear from typical pain and a serum lipase four times normal. A junior doctor requests a contrast CT on the day of admission. When is contrast CT most useful in assessing local complications?
o: Only if serum amylase remains raised
questions.e: Necrosis and fluid collections may not be visible in the first few days, so contrast CT is most informative after about 72 hours in patients who fail to improve, unless the diagnosis is in doubt. Amylase levels do not reflect severity or complications.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man had acute alcohol-related pancreatitis 8 weeks ago. He now has early satiety, epigastric fullness and vomiting after meals. CT shows a 9 cm well-encapsulated homogeneous fluid collection behind the stomach, compressing it, without solid debris. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: A mature, symptomatic pancreatic pseudocyst lying against the stomach is best drained internally by endoscopic cystgastrostomy. Simple percutaneous aspiration has high recurrence, and observation is for small asymptomatic collections, not one causing gastric outlet symptoms.

questions.s: A 52-year-old man with severe acute pancreatitis is in the high-dependency unit. On day 16 he develops new fever and rising inflammatory markers. CT shows 40 % pancreatic necrosis containing gas bubbles. He is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Gas within necrosis indicates infected necrosis, managed with antibiotics and a step-up approach: percutaneous or endoscopic drainage first, then minimally invasive necrosectomy only if needed, ideally after the collection has walled off. Early open necrosectomy has higher mortality and organ failure.

questions.s: A 68-year-old man has 6 weeks of painless, progressive jaundice with dark urine, pale stools and generalised itching. He has lost 7 kg. On examination there is a smooth, non-tender, palpable gallbladder. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Courvoisier's law states that a palpable gallbladder with painless obstructive jaundice is unlikely to be due to stones, pointing to malignant obstruction such as carcinoma of the pancreatic head. Stones cause a fibrosed gallbladder that cannot distend and are usually painful.

questions.s: A 62-year-old woman has painless obstructive jaundice. Ultrasound shows dilated intrahepatic ducts, a dilated common bile duct and a dilated pancreatic duct, but no gallstones and no mass is clearly seen. Which investigation is most appropriate next?
questions.e: A double-duct sign suggests a periampullary or pancreatic head tumour, and pancreatic-protocol contrast CT is the key test to diagnose and stage it and judge resectability. ERCP is invasive and not the first test for diagnosis, and CA 19-9 alone is neither sensitive nor specific.

questions.s: A 59-year-old man has a 2.5 cm adenocarcinoma of the head of the pancreas. Staging CT shows no metastases and no involvement of the superior mesenteric vessels. Which operation is most appropriate?
questions.e: Resectable cancers of the pancreatic head are removed by pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple's operation), usually followed by adjuvant chemotherapy. Distal pancreatectomy is for body and tail tumours, and the Frey and lateral pancreaticojejunostomy procedures are drainage operations for chronic pancreatitis.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man with long-standing alcohol use has recurrent epigastric pain, newly diagnosed diabetes and pale, bulky, offensive stools that are difficult to flush. Abdominal X-ray shows pancreatic calcification. Which treatment will best improve his stools?
questions.e: Steatorrhoea in chronic pancreatitis reflects exocrine insufficiency and is treated with pancreatic enzyme replacement taken with meals and snacks, along with stopping alcohol. A strict fat-free diet worsens malnutrition and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man with severe acute pancreatitis develops bluish discolouration of both flanks on day 3 of his admission. What is this sign called?
questions.e: Flank bruising (Grey Turner's sign) reflects retroperitoneal haemorrhage tracking from the pancreas and suggests severe disease. Cullen's sign is periumbilical bruising, Battle's sign is mastoid bruising in base-of-skull fracture, and Kehr's sign is left shoulder pain in splenic rupture.

questions.s: A 74-year-old man with chronic constipation, living in a care home in Rawalpindi, has 2 days of gross abdominal distension and absolute constipation. He is not peritonitic and lactate is normal. Abdominal X-ray shows a hugely dilated loop of colon arising from the pelvis in a bent inner-tube shape. What is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Insertion of a self-expanding colonic stent
questions.e: Sigmoid volvulus without peritonitis or ischaemia is first decompressed with flexible sigmoidoscopy and a flatus tube; elective resection is then considered because recurrence is common. Emergency surgery is for peritonitis, gangrene or failed decompression, and stents are used for malignant obstruction.

questions.s: A 55-year-old woman who had an abdominal hysterectomy 10 years ago has 24 hours of colicky central abdominal pain, bilious vomiting and distension. She is afebrile, pulse 90/min, the abdomen is soft with no localised tenderness, and lactate is normal. X-ray shows dilated small bowel loops. What is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Immediate laparotomy and division of adhesions
questions.e: Adhesional small bowel obstruction without features of strangulation is managed conservatively with nasogastric decompression, IV fluids and electrolyte correction, often with a water-soluble contrast study. Most settle without surgery; immediate laparotomy is for strangulation or failure of conservative care.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man with adhesional small bowel obstruction has been managed conservatively for 12 hours. His pain has become constant rather than colicky, temperature is 38.3 °C, pulse 118/min and there is localised tenderness with guarding. Lactate has risen to 4.2 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Conservative care for a further 48 hours
questions.e: Constant pain, fever, tachycardia, localised peritonism and rising lactate suggest strangulation, which requires urgent laparotomy after resuscitation. Continuing conservative care or further imaging delays surgery and increases the risk of gangrene and perforation.

questions.s: A 70-year-old woman has 5 days of increasing abdominal distension and absolute constipation. CT shows an obstructing tumour in the descending colon with a competent ileocaecal valve and dilated colon proximal to it; the caecum measures 11 cm and she is tender in the right iliac fossa. Which part of the bowel is at greatest risk of perforation?
questions.e: With a competent ileocaecal valve the obstructed colon forms a closed loop, and by Laplace's law the widest segment, the caecum, has the highest wall tension and perforates first. A caecal diameter over about 10-12 cm with right iliac fossa tenderness is a warning sign needing urgent decompression.

questions.s: An 81-year-old man develops massive abdominal distension 4 days after fixation of a hip fracture. He is on morphine for pain, potassium is 2.9 mmol/L, and he is passing some flatus. The abdomen is soft and non-tender. CT shows a dilated colon to the splenic flexure, caecum 9 cm, with no mechanical obstruction. What is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's syndrome) without signs of ischaemia is first managed conservatively: correct electrolytes, stop opioids and other contributing drugs, and decompress. Neostigmine is a second-line option needing cardiac monitoring because of bradycardia, and surgery is for perforation or ischaemia.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man with adhesional small bowel obstruction has not improved after 48 hours of nasogastric decompression and IV fluids. He is clinically stable without peritonism. He is given oral water-soluble contrast, and an abdominal X-ray 24 hours later shows contrast in the colon. What does this finding indicate?
questions.e: Water-soluble contrast reaching the colon within 24 hours strongly predicts that adhesional obstruction will settle without operation, and the contrast may also speed resolution. Failure of contrast to reach the colon suggests complete obstruction and favours surgery.

questions.s: A supine abdominal X-ray of a patient with vomiting and colicky pain shows multiple centrally placed dilated loops of bowel. The mucosal folds cross the entire width of each loop, giving a stacked-coin appearance. What are these folds?
questions.e: Valvulae conniventes (plicae circulares) of the small bowel cross the full width of the lumen, identifying dilated loops as small bowel. Colonic haustral folds are spaced further apart and do not cross the whole width, and dilated colon lies peripherally.

questions.s: A 72-year-old thin woman, who has never had an operation, presents with 2 days of colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and distension. There is a small, firm, tender, irreducible lump in the right groin below and lateral to the pubic tubercle without a cough impulse. X-ray shows small bowel obstruction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A tender irreducible lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle in an elderly woman with small bowel obstruction is an obstructed femoral hernia, which has a high risk of strangulation because of the narrow femoral ring. An inguinal hernia emerges above and medial to the tubercle, and a saphena varix is soft and compressible with a cough thrill.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man has achalasia confirmed on manometry. Loss of which neurons in the oesophageal wall causes the failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation?
questions.e: Achalasia results from degeneration of inhibitory (nitric oxide and VIP releasing) neurons in the myenteric plexus, so the lower sphincter fails to relax and peristalsis is lost. The submucosal plexus mainly regulates secretion and blood flow rather than motility.

questions.s: A 28-year-old man vomits repeatedly after a night of heavy drinking and then notices streaks of fresh blood in the last few vomits. He has no chest pain, his pulse is 84/min and Hb is 14.1 g/dL. Endoscopy shows a linear mucosal tear at the gastro-oesophageal junction. What is the diagnosis?
questions.e: A linear mucosal tear at the gastro-oesophageal junction after repeated retching is a Mallory-Weiss tear, which usually stops bleeding on its own. Boerhaave syndrome is a full-thickness rupture presenting with severe chest pain and mediastinal air rather than minor haematemesis.

questions.s: Endoscopic biopsy of a lower oesophageal stricture in a 61-year-old man shows adenocarcinoma. Which investigation should be done next to look for distant spread?
questions.e: After histological diagnosis, contrast CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis is the first staging test, detecting liver, lung and nodal metastases; PET-CT and endoscopic ultrasound follow if the disease appears curable. A bone scan is only done for symptoms, and bronchoscopy is mainly for upper and middle third tumours near the airway.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man presents 6 hours after the sudden onset of severe epigastric pain. Erect chest X-ray shows free gas under the diaphragm, and at laparoscopy there is a 5 mm perforation on the anterior wall of the first part of the duodenum. He is stable. What is the most appropriate operative treatment?
questions.e: A perforated duodenal ulcer is closed with an omental patch and the peritoneal cavity is washed out, followed by PPI therapy and H. pylori eradication. Acid-reducing operations such as vagotomy or gastrectomy are rarely needed now that medical therapy is effective.

questions.s: A 48-year-old woman has early satiety and weight loss. Endoscopy shows a rigid, poorly distensible stomach with thickened folds throughout. Biopsy shows diffusely infiltrating cells with intracellular mucin that pushes the nucleus to one side. Which cells are these?
questions.e: Diffuse-type gastric carcinoma (linitis plastica) infiltrates the wall with signet ring cells, whose mucin vacuole displaces the nucleus, producing a rigid leather-bottle stomach. Spindle cells suggest a stromal tumour, and Reed-Sternberg cells belong to Hodgkin lymphoma.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man with gastric outlet obstruction from an antral carcinoma has been vomiting for a week. He is dry, potassium is 2.8 mmol/L, chloride 84 mmol/L and bicarbonate 36 mmol/L. Which IV fluid is most appropriate for initial correction?
questions.e: Hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic alkalosis from gastric losses is corrected with 0.9% sodium chloride, which replaces chloride and volume, with added potassium chloride. Dextrose alone does not replace chloride, and bicarbonate would worsen the alkalosis.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man has a biopsy-proven adenocarcinoma of the rectum 6 cm from the anal verge. CT shows no distant metastases. Which investigation best assesses the local extent of the tumour and its relation to the mesorectal fascia?
questions.e: Pelvic MRI shows the depth of tumour spread, nodal involvement and the distance to the mesorectal fascia (the circumferential resection margin), which decides whether neoadjuvant therapy is needed. CT and PET-CT are less accurate for local staging in the pelvis.

questions.s: A 75-year-old man with aortic stenosis has had several episodes of painless fresh bleeding per rectum and iron-deficiency anaemia over a year. Colonoscopy shows small, flat, cherry-red vascular lesions in the caecum and ascending colon. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Flat cherry-red vascular lesions in the right colon of an elderly patient are angiodysplasia, which causes recurrent painless bleeding and is associated with aortic stenosis. Diverticular bleeding also causes painless bleeding, but it arises from diverticula, which are not described.

questions.s: A 55-year-old woman has episodes of facial flushing, watery diarrhoea and wheeze. Echocardiography shows tricuspid regurgitation. CT shows a small ileal mass and multiple liver lesions. Which test best supports the diagnosis?
questions.e: Flushing, diarrhoea, bronchospasm and right-sided valve disease with an ileal tumour and liver metastases indicate carcinoid syndrome, and raised urinary 5-HIAA (a serotonin metabolite) supports it. Liver metastases allow serotonin to bypass hepatic breakdown, which is why the syndrome appears. Metanephrines and VMA are for phaeochromocytoma.

questions.s: During laparoscopic appendicectomy, the surgeon divides the mesoappendix containing the appendicular artery. This artery is most commonly a branch of which vessel?
questions.e: The appendicular artery arises from the ileocolic artery (often its inferior division) and runs in the free edge of the mesoappendix. Because it is an end artery, thrombosis in appendicitis leads to gangrene and perforation.

questions.s: A 21-year-old man has 20 hours of right iliac fossa pain that began around the umbilicus, anorexia and a temperature of 37.8 °C. He has right iliac fossa guarding, and WBC is 14,200/mm³. Ultrasound shows a non-compressible 9 mm appendix without perforation or collection. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Confirmed uncomplicated acute appendicitis in a fit adult is treated by appendicectomy, usually laparoscopic, with prophylactic antibiotics. Interval appendicectomy applies to appendix masses treated conservatively, and discharge on oral antibiotics without review is unsafe.

questions.s: A 68-year-old man has been treated non-operatively for an appendix mass and has fully recovered. What is the most important next step before discharge from follow-up?
questions.e: In older patients an apparent appendix mass may be a caecal carcinoma, so the colon is examined (colonoscopy or CT) once the inflammation has settled. Surgery within a week of an inflammatory mass is hazardous, and antibiotics have no long-term role.

questions.s: A 38-year-old man has a recurrent anal fistula. Examination under anaesthesia shows a trans-sphincteric tract crossing the upper half of the external sphincter. What is the most appropriate surgical treatment?
o: Excision of the external opening only
questions.e: A high trans-sphincteric fistula cannot be laid open without dividing much of the sphincter and risking incontinence, so a draining seton is placed to control sepsis, followed by a sphincter-sparing procedure if needed. Fistulotomy is suitable for low fistulas involving little sphincter.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man with bleeding internal haemorrhoids asks why they do not hurt, whereas his friend's perianal haematoma was very painful. What is the best explanation for internal haemorrhoids being painless?
o: Supplied by the inferior rectal nerve
Drained by the systemic venous system
questions.e: Internal haemorrhoids arise above the dentate line, where the mucosa has autonomic (visceral) innervation insensitive to cutting and pricking, so they bleed without pain. Below the dentate line the anoderm is supplied by the somatic inferior rectal nerve and is very pain-sensitive.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man has a squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal below the dentate line. Which lymph nodes are the first to receive lymph from this region?
questions.e: Below the dentate line the anal canal drains to the superficial inguinal nodes, so the groins must be examined in anal cancer. The region above the dentate line drains to the internal iliac and inferior mesenteric nodes.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman has had three episodes of right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals, each lasting about 2 hours and settling on its own. Between episodes she is well. Ultrasound shows multiple gallstones with a normal wall and normal duct, and liver function tests are normal. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Reassurance with a low-fat diet only
questions.e: Symptomatic gallstones causing biliary colic are treated with elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy because attacks recur and complications such as cholecystitis and pancreatitis may follow. ERCP is for duct stones, which are not present here.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man in the intensive care unit after major burns develops fever and right upper quadrant tenderness. Ultrasound shows a distended gallbladder with a thickened wall and pericholecystic fluid but no stones. He remains on a ventilator with high oxygen needs. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Acalculous cholecystitis in a critically ill patient is treated with antibiotics and percutaneous cholecystostomy, which drains the gallbladder without general anaesthesia or major surgery. It can progress quickly to gangrene and perforation, so observation is unsafe, and ERCP does not drain the gallbladder reliably.

questions.s: A 14-year-old boy with beta-thalassaemia major, on regular transfusions, has recurrent right upper quadrant pain. Ultrasound shows multiple small gallstones. What type of stones are most likely?
questions.e: Chronic haemolysis increases bilirubin excretion, which precipitates as calcium bilirubinate in the gallbladder forming black pigment stones. Brown pigment stones form in the bile ducts with infection or parasites, and cholesterol stones are typical of obese adults.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman who has taken the combined oral contraceptive pill for 10 years presents with sudden right upper quadrant pain. CT shows a 6 cm well-defined liver lesion with evidence of recent bleeding within it. The liver is otherwise normal, and AFP is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Hepatocellular adenoma is linked to oral contraceptive use and, especially when over 5 cm, can bleed or rupture. Focal nodular hyperplasia is not hormone-driven, has a central scar and rarely bleeds, and HCC is unlikely in a normal liver with normal AFP.

questions.s: A 40-year-old woman has an ultrasound for dyspepsia that shows a 3 cm echogenic liver lesion. Contrast CT shows peripheral nodular enhancement that fills in towards the centre on delayed images. She has no liver disease. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill-in is typical of a cavernous haemangioma, which is benign and needs no treatment when asymptomatic. Biopsy should be avoided because these lesions are vascular and can bleed.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman has ascites and tender hepatomegaly. Doppler ultrasound shows hepatic vein thrombosis, and CT shows the caudate lobe enlarged while the rest of the liver is congested and atrophic. Which anatomical feature explains the sparing and enlargement of the caudate lobe?
questions.e: The caudate lobe (segment I) drains through short veins directly into the inferior vena cava, bypassing the main hepatic veins, so in Budd-Chiari syndrome it remains drained and hypertrophies. Its arterial and biliary supply do not explain this pattern.

questions.s: On day 2 of severe acute pancreatitis, a 49-year-old woman has a corrected serum calcium of 7.2 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5). What is the main mechanism of her hypocalcaemia?
questions.e: Lipase released from the inflamed pancreas breaks down peripancreatic fat, and the free fatty acids bind calcium to form soaps (saponification), lowering serum calcium. Low calcium is a marker of severe pancreatitis in the Glasgow-Imrie score.

questions.s: A 12-year-old boy falls off his bicycle and the handlebar strikes his upper abdomen. A day later he has epigastric pain and a raised serum amylase. CT shows a transection of the pancreas. Where is the pancreas most likely to be divided?
questions.e: A direct epigastric blow compresses the pancreatic neck against the vertebral column behind it, so the neck is the usual site of transection. The head and tail are less exposed to crushing against bone.

questions.s: A 72-year-old man has 3 weeks of worsening constipation and weight loss, and for 2 days has passed no stool or flatus. His abdomen is distended and tympanic. X-ray shows a dilated colon with a cut-off in the left iliac fossa. What is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Colorectal carcinoma is the commonest cause of large bowel obstruction in adults, and progressive change in bowel habit with weight loss before complete obstruction fits a slowly narrowing tumour. Sigmoid volvulus presents more abruptly and produces a large inverted U-shaped loop on X-ray.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man has sudden colicky upper abdominal pain with early, frequent bilious vomiting. His abdomen is only slightly distended and he passed stool earlier that day. Where is the obstruction most likely to be?
questions.e: High (proximal) small bowel obstruction causes early, profuse vomiting with little distension because few loops lie above the block, and the bowel below can still empty. Distal or colonic obstruction causes marked distension, with vomiting later and often faeculent.

questions.s: Hira, a 19-year-old university student, found a painless lump in her left breast a month ago. It is a 2 cm, firm, smooth, well-defined lump that moves freely under the fingers. There is no axillary lymphadenopathy. What is the most appropriate initial imaging?
questions.e: In young women dense breast tissue makes mammography less useful, so ultrasound is the imaging of choice as part of triple assessment; the features suggest a fibroadenoma. Excision is not the first step and is kept for enlarging, large or uncertain lesions.

questions.s: A 52-year-old woman has a hard, irregular 3 cm lump in the upper outer quadrant of her right breast with skin tethering. Mammography shows a spiculated mass. What is the best way to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Image-guided core needle biopsy provides histology, distinguishes invasive from in-situ cancer and allows hormone receptor and HER2 testing before planning treatment. Fine-needle aspiration gives cytology only, and tumour markers are not diagnostic.

questions.s: A 26-year-old woman who is breastfeeding her 3-week-old baby has a painful, red, swollen area in the left breast and fever of 38.6 °C despite 3 days of oral flucloxacillin. Ultrasound shows a 3 cm fluid collection. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Incision and drainage with packing under GA
Continue the same antibiotics for 2 weeks
questions.e: A lactational breast abscess is first treated by ultrasound-guided needle aspiration (repeated if needed) with antibiotics, and breastfeeding or expressing should continue to drain the breast. Open drainage leaves a larger scar and is reserved for failure of aspiration or skin necrosis.

questions.s: A 58-year-old woman has had a red, scaly, itchy rash on her right nipple for 4 months that has not improved with steroid cream. The nipple is now partly eroded, while the areola beyond it is less affected. The left nipple is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A unilateral eczema-like rash that starts on the nipple, destroys it and fails to respond to steroids suggests Paget's disease of the nipple, which usually indicates an underlying carcinoma and needs biopsy and mammography. Eczema is usually bilateral, starts on the areola and spares the nipple.

questions.s: A 40-year-old woman notices spontaneous blood-stained discharge from a single duct of her left nipple. There is no palpable lump, and pressing at the 3 o'clock position of the areola reproduces the discharge. Mammography is normal. What is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Bloody discharge from a single duct in a woman of this age is most often due to an intraductal papilloma, which still needs imaging and usually excision to exclude carcinoma. Duct ectasia typically causes thick, greenish discharge from several ducts in older women.
