questions.s: A 50-year-old woman has a firm, irregular 2 cm lump in her left breast with slight skin dimpling. She recalls severe bruising across the breast from a seat belt in a road accident 2 months ago. Mammography shows an irregular mass with a lucent centre and curvilinear calcification. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A firm irregular lump after trauma, with an oil cyst or calcified rim on mammography, suggests fat necrosis. It can mimic carcinoma clinically, so triple assessment including biopsy is still completed before reassurance.

questions.s: A 45-year-old woman has a smooth, mobile breast lump that has grown from 3 cm to 8 cm in 4 months, stretching the overlying skin. Core biopsy shows a leaf-like stromal proliferation with increased stromal cellularity, consistent with a phyllodes tumour. The axilla is clinically normal. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Wide local excision with clear margins
Modified radical mastectomy with axillary clearance
questions.e: Phyllodes tumours tend to recur locally, so they are excised with a clear margin of normal tissue (mastectomy only if the breast cannot be preserved). They rarely spread to lymph nodes, so axillary surgery is not needed, and enucleation leaves tumour behind.

questions.s: A 48-year-old woman has a 2 cm invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast. There are no palpable axillary nodes, and axillary ultrasound is normal. She is planned for wide local excision. How should the axilla be staged?
questions.e: In a clinically and sonographically negative axilla, sentinel lymph node biopsy stages the axilla with far less lymphoedema and shoulder morbidity than clearance. Axillary clearance is used when nodes are proven involved, and omitting staging would leave prognosis and adjuvant treatment uncertain.

questions.s: A 38-year-old premenopausal woman has had a wide local excision and sentinel node biopsy for invasive breast cancer. Histology shows strong oestrogen receptor positivity and HER2 negativity. Which adjuvant endocrine therapy is most appropriate?
questions.e: Tamoxifen blocks oestrogen receptors and is effective whatever the menopausal status, making it standard for premenopausal ER-positive cancer. An aromatase inhibitor alone is ineffective while the ovaries are working, and trastuzumab is only for HER2-positive disease.

questions.s: A 45-year-old woman with HER2-positive breast cancer is starting adjuvant trastuzumab. Which test should be done before and at regular intervals during treatment?
questions.e: Trastuzumab can reduce left ventricular function, so the ejection fraction is checked by echocardiography (or MUGA) at baseline and during treatment. The cardiotoxicity is usually reversible on stopping, unlike anthracycline damage.

questions.s: A 44-year-old woman who is not breastfeeding has had a red, warm, swollen right breast for 4 weeks. The skin over more than a third of the breast has a pitted orange-peel appearance. She has no fever, and two courses of antibiotics have not helped. A firm axillary node is palpable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Diffuse erythema, oedema and peau d'orange over a large part of the breast, without fever and unresponsive to antibiotics, suggest inflammatory breast cancer, caused by tumour emboli in dermal lymphatics. Mastitis and abscess outside lactation usually cause fever, localised tenderness and respond to antibiotics or drainage.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman attends a breast clinic in Lahore. Her mother had breast cancer at 41, her sister at 38, and her maternal aunt died of ovarian cancer. A germline mutation in which gene is most likely in this family?
questions.e: Early-onset breast cancer in several relatives combined with ovarian cancer is typical of BRCA1 (or BRCA2) mutation. TP53 (Li-Fraumeni syndrome) causes early breast cancer with sarcomas, brain tumours and adrenal carcinoma rather than ovarian cancer.

questions.s: A 34-year-old woman has a 2 cm painless nodule in the right lobe of the thyroid found by her GP. She feels well, and serum TSH is normal. There is no lymphadenopathy. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: With a normal TSH, ultrasound characterises the nodule and identifies suspicious features that decide whether ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration is needed. Isotope scanning is useful only when TSH is suppressed, to look for a hot nodule.

questions.s: A 42-year-old woman has a 3 cm thyroid nodule, palpitations and weight loss. Serum TSH is below 0.01 mU/L and free T4 is raised. What is the most appropriate next investigation for the nodule?
questions.e: A nodule with suppressed TSH may be an autonomous toxic adenoma, and an isotope scan showing a hot nodule with suppressed surrounding gland confirms it. Hot nodules are rarely malignant, so FNA is generally not needed, and cytology of hyperfunctioning nodules can be misleading.

questions.s: A 48-year-old woman has weight loss and palpitations. There is a single smooth 3 cm nodule in the right lobe of the thyroid. TSH is suppressed and free T4 raised. A technetium scan shows intense uptake in the nodule with suppressed uptake in the rest of the gland. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A single hot nodule that takes up isotope while the rest of the gland is suppressed is a toxic (autonomous) adenoma; hot nodules are rarely malignant. Graves disease gives diffuse increased uptake across the whole gland, and papillary carcinoma usually appears as a cold nodule in a euthyroid patient.

questions.s: A 40-year-old woman has a 3 cm solitary thyroid nodule with normal TSH. Ultrasound-guided FNA is reported as a follicular neoplasm (cellular follicular lesion without papillary features). Ultrasound shows no lymph node involvement. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.e: Cytology cannot distinguish follicular adenoma from carcinoma because the distinction depends on capsular or vascular invasion, so a diagnostic hemithyroidectomy provides histology. Completion thyroidectomy follows if carcinoma is confirmed; radioiodine is only given after total thyroidectomy for cancer.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man has a thyroid nodule and intermittent diarrhoea. Serum calcitonin is markedly raised. His father had an adrenal tumour removed for episodic hypertension. Before thyroid surgery, which investigation is essential?
questions.e: Medullary thyroid carcinoma with a family history of adrenal tumour suggests MEN2, and a coexisting phaeochromocytoma must be excluded and treated first, because operating on the thyroid with an untreated phaeochromocytoma can provoke a fatal hypertensive crisis. Thyroglobulin is a marker for differentiated follicular-cell cancers, not medullary cancer.

questions.s: The day after a left hemithyroidectomy, a 45-year-old woman has a hoarse, breathy voice and coughs when drinking water. Laryngoscopy shows the left vocal cord fixed near the midline. Which nerve has most likely been injured?
o: External branch of the superior laryngeal
questions.e: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid, so injury paralyses the vocal cord, causing hoarseness and aspiration. Injury to the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve affects cricothyroid and causes loss of high-pitched voice and voice fatigue rather than a fixed cord.

questions.s: Thirty-six hours after a total thyroidectomy for Graves' disease, a 34-year-old woman complains of tingling around her mouth and in her fingers. Her hand goes into spasm when a BP cuff is inflated. Corrected calcium is 6.8 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5). What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
questions.e: Symptomatic hypocalcaemia with tetany (Trousseau's sign) after thyroidectomy, usually from parathyroid injury or devascularisation, is treated urgently with slow IV calcium gluconate under cardiac monitoring, then oral calcium and active vitamin D. Oral therapy alone acts too slowly for symptomatic tetany.

questions.s: Four hours after a total thyroidectomy, a 50-year-old woman becomes restless with stridor. The neck is tense and swollen beneath the dressing, and her oxygen saturation is falling. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Open the wound at the bedside
Urgent CT scan of the neck first
questions.e: A tense neck haematoma after thyroidectomy compresses the airway and venous drainage, so the skin and strap muscle sutures must be opened immediately at the bedside to release the clot, before return to theatre. Intubation through an oedematous, distorted airway is difficult and delays decompression, and imaging wastes critical time.

questions.s: A 32-year-old woman with Graves' disease is listed for total thyroidectomy. She has been made euthyroid on carbimazole. Which drug is often given for about 10 days before surgery to reduce the vascularity of the gland?
questions.e: Potassium iodide (Lugol's iodine) given for about 10 days before surgery reduces thyroid blood flow and makes the gland firmer, lowering blood loss. Propranolol controls adrenergic symptoms but does not reduce vascularity, and radioactive iodine is an alternative treatment rather than preparation for surgery.

questions.s: A 76-year-old woman with a long-standing nodular goitre notices that it has grown rapidly over 6 weeks. It is now hard, fixed and tender, and she has hoarseness and difficulty breathing. Core biopsy shows highly pleomorphic giant and spindle cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Rapid growth of a hard, fixed mass with local invasion in an elderly patient, with undifferentiated pleomorphic and giant cells on biopsy, indicates anaplastic carcinoma, which carries a very poor prognosis. Haemorrhage into a cyst causes sudden painful swelling but not a hard, fixed infiltrating mass.

questions.s: A 68-year-old woman has a large multinodular goitre and breathlessness when lying flat. When she raises both arms above her head, her face becomes congested within a minute. The lower border of the goitre cannot be felt. Which investigation best assesses the extent of the goitre and tracheal compression?
o: CT of the neck and thorax
questions.e: Pemberton's sign and an impalpable lower border suggest retrosternal extension, and CT of the neck and thorax shows the extent into the mediastinum and the degree of tracheal narrowing for surgical planning. Ultrasound cannot see behind the sternum.

questions.s: A thyroid surgeon operating on a professional singer takes care to ligate one vessel close to the upper pole of the thyroid gland, so as not to injure the nerve that runs with it and allows high-pitched notes. Which vessel is this?
questions.e: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery to supply cricothyroid, which tenses the vocal cords for high notes, so the artery is ligated close to the gland. The recurrent laryngeal nerve is related to the inferior thyroid artery instead.

questions.s: A 55-year-old woman has recurrent renal stones and vague aches. Serum calcium is 11.6 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5), phosphate is low, and parathyroid hormone is raised. What is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.e: Hypercalcaemia with a raised PTH is primary hyperparathyroidism, which is caused by a single adenoma in about 85 % of cases. Hyperplasia accounts for most of the rest, and carcinoma is rare; malignancy-related hypercalcaemia usually suppresses PTH.

questions.s: A 60-year-old woman has primary hyperparathyroidism confirmed biochemically and is referred for parathyroidectomy. The surgeon wants to locate the abnormal gland before operating so that a focused approach can be used. Which investigation is most useful, together with neck ultrasound?
questions.e: Sestamibi is retained longer by hyperfunctioning parathyroid tissue than by thyroid, so a sestamibi scan combined with ultrasound localises most adenomas and allows a minimally invasive operation. Localisation is for planning surgery, not for making the diagnosis, which is biochemical.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man has mild hypercalcaemia (calcium 10.9 mg/dL, normal 8.5-10.5) found on routine testing, with a PTH at the upper end of normal. He has no symptoms. His mother and brother also have raised calcium, and his brother had a neck exploration that found no adenoma. Which test should be done before any surgery?
questions.e: Lifelong mild hypercalcaemia in several relatives with normal or slightly raised PTH suggests familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, confirmed by a very low urinary calcium:creatinine clearance ratio. It is benign and does not need parathyroidectomy, which explains the brother's negative exploration.

questions.s: A 65-year-old woman with known primary hyperparathyroidism is brought in confused and vomiting. She is clinically dehydrated, and corrected serum calcium is 15.1 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5). What is the most appropriate first step in management?
questions.e: Severe hypercalcaemia causes polyuria and dehydration, so the first step is IV rehydration with 0.9% saline, which also increases calcium excretion; a bisphosphonate is added once she is rehydrated. Loop diuretics before rehydration worsen volume depletion, and surgery follows once she is stable.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man on haemodialysis for 6 years has bone pain and itching. Serum calcium is 8.2 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5), phosphate is 7.1 mg/dL (normal 2.5-4.5), and PTH is markedly raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: In chronic kidney disease, phosphate retention and reduced vitamin D activation lower calcium and drive the parathyroids to hypersecrete, giving secondary hyperparathyroidism with low or normal calcium. Tertiary hyperparathyroidism is when the glands become autonomous and calcium rises.

questions.s: A 38-year-old man had a successful kidney transplant 18 months ago after many years on dialysis. His graft function is good, but serum calcium is now 11.5 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5), phosphate is low and PTH remains very high. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: After long-standing secondary hyperparathyroidism, hyperplastic glands may keep secreting PTH autonomously even when the stimulus is removed, causing hypercalcaemia: tertiary hyperparathyroidism. Secondary hyperparathyroidism has low or normal calcium, and the long renal history points away from a new primary disorder.

questions.s: A 34-year-old man has recurrent duodenal ulcers despite treatment, kidney stones with hypercalcaemia and a raised PTH, and an MRI showing a pituitary adenoma. Which syndrome is most likely?
questions.e: Parathyroid hyperplasia, pituitary adenoma and a pancreatic or duodenal gastrinoma (causing refractory ulcers) are the classic triad of MEN1. MEN2A combines medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism, but not pituitary or gastrin-secreting tumours.

questions.s: A 58-year-old woman with severe primary hyperparathyroidism and a high alkaline phosphatase from bone disease has a parathyroid adenoma removed. On day 3 she has tingling and cramps. Calcium is 7.0 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5), phosphate and magnesium are both low, and PTH is in the normal range. What is the most likely mechanism?
o: Rapid uptake of calcium into bone
questions.e: Hungry bone syndrome follows removal of a long-standing adenoma: demineralised bone rapidly takes up calcium, phosphate and magnesium, causing prolonged hypocalcaemia with low phosphate. Hypoparathyroidism from gland damage gives a low PTH and a high phosphate instead.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman has episodes of severe headache, palpitations, sweating and pallor lasting 15-20 minutes. During one attack her BP was 210/120 mmHg; between attacks it is 150/95 mmHg. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Paroxysmal headache, palpitations and sweating with hypertension suggest phaeochromocytoma, and the first step is biochemical confirmation with plasma free (or urinary fractionated) metanephrines. Imaging such as CT or MIBG is done only after biochemistry is positive, to avoid chasing incidental adrenal lesions.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man has a 4 cm right adrenal phaeochromocytoma confirmed biochemically and on CT. He is listed for laparoscopic adrenalectomy. Which drug should be started first to prepare him for surgery?
questions.e: Alpha-blockade with phenoxybenzamine (or doxazosin) for 1-2 weeks controls BP and allows volume re-expansion before surgery. A beta-blocker is added only after alpha-blockade, because beta-blockade alone leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and can precipitate a hypertensive crisis.

questions.s: A 42-year-old man has hypertension that remains uncontrolled on three drugs. Serum potassium is 2.9 mmol/L, and bicarbonate is 32 mmol/L. He takes no diuretics. What is the most appropriate screening test?
questions.e: Resistant hypertension with spontaneous hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis suggests primary hyperaldosteronism, screened with the plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio. Metanephrines screen for phaeochromocytoma, and dexamethasone suppression for Cushing's syndrome.

questions.s: A 50-year-old woman has confirmed primary hyperaldosteronism. CT shows a 1.5 cm nodule in the left adrenal gland and a normal right gland. She is keen on surgery. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.e: Non-functioning adrenal nodules are common in older patients, and CT cannot reliably show which gland is producing excess aldosterone, so adrenal vein sampling confirms lateralisation before unilateral adrenalectomy. If secretion is bilateral (hyperplasia) treatment is medical with a mineralocorticoid antagonist, not surgery.

questions.s: A 55-year-old woman has a CT for abdominal pain that incidentally shows a 2.5 cm homogeneous left adrenal lesion with attenuation of 6 Hounsfield units. She is normotensive and has no features of hormone excess. Which test should be performed in her case?
questions.e: Every adrenal incidentaloma needs hormonal evaluation, and a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test is done in all to exclude autonomous cortisol secretion; low attenuation (under 10 HU) indicates a lipid-rich benign adenoma. Biopsy is not used to assess adrenal masses because it is unhelpful and can seed tumour or provoke a crisis in phaeochromocytoma.

questions.s: A 52-year-old man has an incidental 6 cm heterogeneous right adrenal mass on CT with an unenhanced attenuation of 35 Hounsfield units. Hormonal tests, including metanephrines, are normal. There is no known cancer elsewhere. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Large size (over 4 cm) and high attenuation with heterogeneity raise concern for adrenocortical carcinoma, so the mass should be removed. Observation risks progression, and biopsy cannot reliably distinguish adenoma from carcinoma and may seed tumour.

questions.s: A 38-year-old woman has Cushing's syndrome from a 3 cm left adrenal adenoma; ACTH is suppressed. She undergoes laparoscopic left adrenalectomy. Why does she need hydrocortisone replacement after the operation?
o: Damage to the pituitary during surgery
questions.e: Long-standing cortisol excess suppresses ACTH, so the remaining adrenal gland is atrophied and cannot produce enough cortisol after the adenoma is removed; replacement continues until the axis recovers, often over months. Nelson's syndrome follows bilateral adrenalectomy for pituitary Cushing's disease, not unilateral surgery for an adenoma.

questions.s: During a right adrenalectomy, the surgeon warns the assistant that the right adrenal vein is very short and easily torn. Into which vessel does the right adrenal vein drain?
questions.e: The short right adrenal vein drains directly into the posterior aspect of the inferior vena cava, so tearing it causes brisk caval bleeding. The left adrenal vein is longer and drains into the left renal vein.

questions.s: A 45-year-old woman notices a smooth, tender lump in her right breast that appeared over a week. Ultrasound shows a 2.5 cm simple cyst. Aspiration yields 8 mL of clear yellowish-green fluid, and the lump disappears completely. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.e: A simple cyst that yields non-bloody fluid and disappears completely after aspiration needs no further investigation beyond clinical review. Cytology is only sent if the fluid is blood-stained, and a residual lump or rapid refilling needs further assessment.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman has bilateral breast heaviness and pain that starts a week before each period and settles with menstruation. Breast examination and her history are otherwise normal. What is the most appropriate first-line management?
questions.e: Cyclical mastalgia with a normal examination is hormonal and benign, and most women improve with reassurance, a well-fitting supportive bra and simple analgesia. Tamoxifen and danazol have significant side effects and are reserved for severe refractory cases under specialist care.

questions.s: A 20-year-old university student in Lahore has a painless lump in her left breast that she noticed 3 months ago. It is 2 cm, smooth, rubbery and very mobile under the fingers. There is no nipple discharge or axillary lymphadenopathy, and ultrasound shows a well-defined oval solid lesion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A smooth, rubbery, highly mobile solid lump in a young woman is typically a fibroadenoma, confirmed by triple assessment with core biopsy if there is any doubt. A phyllodes tumour usually occurs in women aged 40-50 and grows rapidly to a large size, and a cyst is anechoic rather than solid on ultrasound.

questions.s: A 65-year-old woman with long-standing Hashimoto's thyroiditis on levothyroxine notices that her goitre has enlarged rapidly over 2 months and feels rubbery. She has mild dysphagia. Core biopsy shows sheets of monoclonal B lymphocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Primary thyroid lymphoma usually arises in a gland affected by Hashimoto's thyroiditis and presents as a rapidly enlarging goitre in an older woman; it is mainly treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy rather than surgery. Subacute thyroiditis causes a painful tender gland after a viral illness.

questions.s: A 36-year-old woman has had a total thyroidectomy and radioiodine ablation for papillary carcinoma. Which serum marker is used to detect recurrence during follow-up?
questions.e: After total thyroidectomy and ablation there should be no thyroid tissue left to make thyroglobulin, so a detectable or rising level suggests recurrence of differentiated thyroid cancer. Calcitonin and CEA are markers for medullary carcinoma.

questions.s: A 60-year-old woman presents with a pathological fracture of the femur. Biopsy of the bone lesion shows well-formed thyroid follicles. Examination reveals a thyroid nodule. Which thyroid cancer most commonly spreads in this way?
questions.e: Follicular carcinoma invades blood vessels and typically spreads through the bloodstream to bone and lung. Papillary carcinoma mainly spreads through lymphatics to cervical lymph nodes.

questions.s: After a total parathyroidectomy, a doctor taps over the facial nerve in front of the patient's ear, and the corner of the mouth twitches. What is this sign called?
questions.e: Twitching of facial muscles on tapping the facial nerve (Chvostek's sign) shows neuromuscular irritability from hypocalcaemia. Trousseau's sign is carpal spasm when a BP cuff is inflated, which is a more specific sign of hypocalcaemia.

questions.s: During a neck exploration for primary hyperparathyroidism, the surgeon finds only three normal parathyroid glands. The missing inferior gland is eventually found within the thymus in the upper mediastinum. From which embryological structure do the inferior parathyroid glands develop?
questions.e: The inferior parathyroids arise from the third pharyngeal pouch together with the thymus and descend with it, which is why ectopic inferior glands are found in the thymus or mediastinum. The superior glands come from the fourth pouch and are more constant in position.

questions.s: A 62-year-old man with primary hyperparathyroidism has a serum calcium of 13.8 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5). Which ECG change is most characteristic of hypercalcaemia?
questions.e: Hypercalcaemia shortens the plateau of the action potential, producing a short QT interval. A prolonged QT interval is seen in hypocalcaemia, peaked T waves in hyperkalaemia and U waves in hypokalaemia.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man has bilateral adrenal phaeochromocytomas. Eye examination shows retinal haemangioblastomas, and imaging shows multiple renal cysts and a cerebellar lesion. Which syndrome is most likely?
questions.e: Phaeochromocytoma with retinal and cerebellar haemangioblastomas and renal cysts (with a risk of renal cell carcinoma) indicates von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. Neurofibromatosis type 1 is also linked to phaeochromocytoma but presents with café-au-lait spots and neurofibromas.

questions.s: A 36-year-old woman has gained weight centrally over a year and has purple abdominal striae, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness and new hypertension. She takes no steroid medicines. What is the most appropriate initial test to confirm cortisol excess?
o: Contrast-enhanced CT of the adrenal glands
questions.e: Cushing's syndrome is first confirmed biochemically, and failure of cortisol to suppress after overnight low-dose dexamethasone is a standard first test (late-night salivary cortisol or 24-hour urinary free cortisol are alternatives). A random cortisol is unhelpful because of diurnal variation, and ACTH and imaging are used only after confirmation to find the source.

questions.s: A 44-year-old woman who was well prepared with alpha-blockade has a left adrenal phaeochromocytoma removed laparoscopically. An hour later her BP is 80/50 mmHg and pulse 104/min. Haemoglobin is unchanged, the drain is dry and there is no rash or wheeze. What is the most likely cause of her hypotension?
o: Adrenal insufficiency from the remaining gland
questions.e: After the tumour is removed, catecholamine levels fall abruptly while alpha-blockade persists, causing vasodilatation and hypotension that respond to IV fluids and sometimes vasopressors. With a stable haemoglobin and dry drain, haemorrhage is unlikely, and a normal contralateral adrenal maintains cortisol after unilateral adrenalectomy for phaeochromocytoma.

questions.s: Kashif, a 35-year-old man, presents to the emergency department in Hyderabad with sudden severe colicky pain in the left loin radiating to the groin for 3 hours. He is restless, afebrile, and urine dipstick shows blood 2+. Abdomen is soft. Which investigation best confirms the diagnosis?
o: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis, delayed phase
Non-contrast CT of kidneys, ureters and bladder
questions.e: Loin-to-groin colic with haematuria suggests ureteric colic, and non-contrast CT KUB is the most sensitive and specific test for urinary stones. Contrast would obscure stones lying in the collecting system, and the intravenous urogram has been replaced because it is less sensitive and needs contrast.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man has right ureteric colic. CT KUB shows a 4 mm stone in the distal ureter with mild hydronephrosis. He is afebrile, pain is controlled with an NSAID, creatinine is normal and urine shows no nitrites or leucocytes. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Analgesia and tamsulosin with follow-up imaging
Ureteroscopy and laser lithotripsy within 24 hours
questions.e: Small distal ureteric stones (under about 5 mm) usually pass spontaneously, and an alpha blocker helps expulsion while analgesia controls pain. Intervention such as ureteroscopy is kept for stones that fail to pass, uncontrolled pain, infection or renal impairment, none of which is present.

questions.s: Nasreen, 45, has right loin pain, rigors and a temperature of 39.4 °C. BP is 96/60 mmHg. CT KUB shows an 8 mm stone in the upper right ureter with moderate hydronephrosis. Blood cultures are taken. What is the most appropriate next step besides intravenous antibiotics?
o: Urgent decompression with a percutaneous nephrostomy
Emergency extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy of the stone
Elective ureteroscopy on the next list
questions.e: An infected obstructed kidney is a urological emergency: drainage by nephrostomy or ureteric stent plus antibiotics is needed urgently to prevent septic shock. Definitive stone treatment such as lithotripsy is deferred until the infection has settled, because fragmenting an infected stone can worsen sepsis.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man with no medical history presents with typical renal colic. Renal function is normal and he has no history of peptic ulcer or asthma. Which analgesic is first-line?
questions.e: NSAIDs such as diclofenac are first-line for renal colic: they relieve pain well and reduce ureteric spasm and renal capsular pressure. Opioids are reserved for when NSAIDs are contraindicated or insufficient, and antispasmodics add little benefit.

questions.s: A 50-year-old woman with recurrent urinary tract infections has a large branched stone filling the renal pelvis and calyces. Urine culture grows Proteus mirabilis. What is the most likely composition of the stone?
questions.e: Staghorn calculi associated with urease-producing organisms such as Proteus are struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones. Urease splits urea into ammonia, making the urine alkaline, which favours struvite precipitation; calcium oxalate stones are commoner overall but are not linked to urease-producing infection.

questions.s: A 58-year-old man with gout has a 9 mm renal pelvis stone that is not visible on a plain X-ray but is seen on CT. His urine pH is 5.0. Which treatment can dissolve this stone?
o: Ammonium chloride to acidify the urine
Potassium citrate to alkalinise the urine
A low calcium diet and a high fluid intake
questions.e: A radiolucent stone in a gout patient with acidic urine is a uric acid stone, and uric acid stones dissolve when the urine is alkalinised to pH 6.5–7 with potassium citrate. Acidifying the urine would worsen uric acid precipitation, and thiazides or calcium restriction target calcium stones.

questions.s: A 42-year-old man has a 2.5 cm stone in the left renal pelvis causing recurrent pain. Renal function is normal and there is no infection. What is the preferred treatment?
questions.e: Renal stones larger than 2 cm are best treated by percutaneous nephrolithotomy, which gives the highest stone-free rate. Shock wave lithotripsy works best for smaller stones and leaves many fragments with large ones, while open surgery is rarely needed now.

questions.s: A 38-year-old man has had three calcium oxalate stones in 4 years. Serum calcium and PTH are normal, and 24-hour urine shows hypercalciuria. Despite drinking more water he forms another stone. Which drug reduces his urinary calcium excretion?
questions.e: Thiazide diuretics increase calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule and so reduce urinary calcium, which lowers recurrence of calcium stones in idiopathic hypercalciuria. Loop diuretics such as furosemide do the opposite and increase calcium excretion.

questions.s: A 16-year-old boy has his second ureteric stone. His elder brother also forms stones. Urine microscopy shows flat hexagonal crystals and the cyanide-nitroprusside test is positive. What is the underlying defect?
o: Defective renal tubular reabsorption of dibasic amino acids
Failure of distal tubular hydrogen ion secretion
questions.e: Hexagonal crystals and a positive nitroprusside test indicate cystinuria, an autosomal recessive defect of renal tubular (and intestinal) transport of cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine. Distal renal tubular acidosis also causes stones in the young, but these are calcium phosphate stones without hexagonal crystals.

questions.s: Ghulam Rasool, 66, has a 1-year history of poor stream, hesitancy and nocturia twice a night. DRE shows a smooth, moderately enlarged prostate. Urinalysis, creatinine and PSA are normal and post-void residual volume is 60 mL. He wants treatment. What is the most appropriate first-line drug?
questions.e: Moderate to severe voiding symptoms from benign prostatic enlargement are treated first with an alpha-1 blocker such as tamsulosin, which relaxes prostatic smooth muscle and works within days. Finasteride is added or used when the prostate is large, and works over months rather than days.

questions.s: A 70-year-old man with lower urinary tract symptoms has an estimated prostate volume of 70 mL on ultrasound and a normal PSA for age. He asks for a drug that will shrink the prostate and reduce his long-term risk of acute retention and surgery. Which drug fits this request?
questions.e: 5-alpha reductase inhibitors such as finasteride block conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, shrink the prostate over 6 months or more, and lower the risk of retention and surgery in large glands. Tamsulosin improves symptoms quickly but does not reduce prostate size.

questions.s: A 68-year-old man has taken tamsulosin for benign prostatic hyperplasia for 2 years. He is now listed for cataract surgery. Which complication should the eye surgeon be warned about because of this drug?
questions.e: Alpha-1A blockade relaxes the iris dilator muscle, causing intraoperative floppy iris syndrome with a billowing iris and poor pupil dilation during cataract surgery. The surgeon should be told in advance so the technique can be adapted; stopping the drug shortly before surgery does not reliably prevent it.

questions.s: A 64-year-old man has taken finasteride for 1 year. His current PSA is 2.1 ng/mL. How should this value be interpreted when assessing his risk of prostate cancer?
o: It should be doubled, as finasteride halves PSA
It should be halved, as finasteride doubles PSA
It needs no correction, as finasteride does not affect PSA
It should be ignored, as PSA is unreliable on finasteride
questions.e: After about 6 months of a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor, the PSA falls by roughly half, so the measured value is doubled for interpretation. A rising PSA on finasteride remains a useful warning sign and should not be ignored.

questions.s: A 72-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia has had two episodes of acute urinary retention in 6 months, each failing a trial without catheter despite tamsulosin. Ultrasound shows a 2 cm bladder stone and normal upper tracts. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Add finasteride and repeat the trial without a catheter in two weeks
Transurethral resection of the prostate with removal of the stone
questions.e: Recurrent retention and bladder stones secondary to obstruction are absolute indications for surgery, and TURP relieves the obstruction while the stone can be removed endoscopically at the same time. More medical therapy has already failed, and a long-term catheter is for men unfit for surgery.

questions.s: During a long transurethral resection of the prostate under spinal anaesthesia using glycine irrigation, a 75-year-old man becomes confused and nauseated. His pulse is 48/min and BP 90/55 mmHg. What is the most likely cause?
o: Dilutional hyponatraemia from absorbed irrigation fluid
Acute haemolytic reaction to an intraoperative transfusion
questions.e: TURP syndrome results from absorption of large volumes of hypotonic irrigant through opened prostatic venous sinuses, causing fluid overload and dilutional hyponatraemia, which present with confusion, bradycardia and hypotension. A high spinal block causes hypotension early after injection, not confusion late in a long resection.

questions.s: A 67-year-old man with lower urinary tract symptoms is examined by digital rectal examination. Which finding most suggests prostate cancer rather than benign enlargement?
o: A smooth, rubbery, symmetrically enlarged gland
A palpable median sulcus with mobile rectal mucosa
questions.e: Carcinoma arises mostly in the peripheral zone, which is felt on rectal examination as a hard, irregular nodule that may obliterate the median sulcus. A smooth, rubbery enlarged gland is typical of benign hyperplasia, and a tender boggy gland suggests acute prostatitis.

questions.s: Benign prostatic hyperplasia causes urinary obstruction because of its site of origin within the gland. In which zone of the prostate does it mainly arise?
questions.e: Benign hyperplasia arises in the transition zone surrounding the prostatic urethra, which is why it compresses the urethra and causes voiding symptoms. Most carcinomas arise in the peripheral zone, which is why they are palpable on rectal examination and cause symptoms late.

questions.s: Abdul Sattar, 74, cannot pass urine for 10 hours after taking a cold remedy. He is in severe suprapubic pain and a tender, dull mass rises to near the umbilicus. He has had poor stream for years. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
o: Start tamsulosin and reassess in 6 hours
Request an urgent ultrasound of the kidneys
Arrange emergency transurethral resection of the prostate
questions.e: Acute painful retention needs immediate bladder drainage, normally with a urethral catheter, and the residual volume is recorded. Investigations and alpha blockers follow after drainage; surgery is not done as an emergency for a first episode.

questions.s: A 19-year-old man slips while crossing a metal beam on a building site and lands astride it. He has perineal pain, a little blood at the urethral meatus and difficulty passing urine. There is a butterfly-shaped bruise in the perineum and scrotum. Which part of the urethra is most likely injured?
questions.e: A straddle injury crushes the bulbar urethra against the pubic arch; extravasated blood and urine are confined by Colles fascia, giving a butterfly perineal bruise. Membranous and prostatic urethral injuries are associated with pelvic fractures rather than falls astride.

questions.s: An 80-year-old man has painless dribbling incontinence. He has a palpable bladder, creatinine 3.4 mg/dL (0.7–1.3) and bilateral hydronephrosis. A urethral catheter drains 1,800 mL. Over the next 24 hours, which complication must he be monitored for most closely?
o: Post-obstructive diuresis with fluid and electrolyte loss
questions.e: Relief of high-pressure chronic retention with renal impairment can cause a large post-obstructive diuresis, leading to dehydration, hypotension and electrolyte disturbance, so urine output, fluid balance and electrolytes must be monitored closely. Renal function usually improves rather than worsens after drainage.

questions.s: A 34-year-old man presents in acute urinary retention. He was treated for gonococcal urethritis 5 years ago and has had a thin, spraying stream since. Two attempts at urethral catheterisation by the registrar meet a firm obstruction in the penile urethra. What is the most appropriate step to drain the bladder?
o: Force a stiffer catheter through the obstruction
Start tamsulosin and wait for spontaneous voiding
questions.e: The history suggests a post-infective urethral stricture, and when urethral catheterisation fails the bladder is drained with a suprapubic catheter. Forcing a catheter risks creating a false passage, and definitive stricture surgery such as urethroplasty is planned electively after imaging.

questions.s: A 69-year-old man with mild prostatic symptoms develops acute urinary retention one week after starting a new medicine for chronic neuropathic pain and poor sleep. Which drug is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Tricyclic antidepressants such as amitriptyline have strong anticholinergic effects that reduce detrusor contraction and can precipitate retention in men with prostatic enlargement. Pregabalin may cause dizziness and oedema but is not a typical cause of retention.

questions.s: A 71-year-old man is catheterised for a first episode of acute urinary retention due to benign prostatic hyperplasia. He wishes to avoid surgery. Which measure most improves the chance of a successful trial without catheter?
o: Starting finasteride and removing the catheter after 1 week
Keeping the catheter in place for 6 weeks to rest the detrusor muscle
Starting an alpha blocker for 2–3 days before catheter removal
questions.e: Starting an alpha blocker such as tamsulosin at catheterisation and removing the catheter after a few days increases the chance of voiding successfully. Finasteride takes months to work, and long catheterisation raises the risk of infection without improving outcome.

questions.s: Hamza, 15, wakes with sudden severe pain in the left testis and vomits twice. Pain started 3 hours ago. The left testis is tender, high-riding with a horizontal lie, and the cremasteric reflex is absent. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Scrotal Doppler ultrasound first, then decide
Urgent surgical exploration of the scrotum
Analgesia and review in the morning
questions.e: Sudden testicular pain with a high-riding horizontal testis and absent cremasteric reflex in an adolescent is testicular torsion until proven otherwise, and urgent exploration should not be delayed for imaging. Salvage falls steeply after about 6 hours of ischaemia, and a normal-looking Doppler does not exclude torsion.

questions.s: A 13-year-old boy is explored for testicular torsion. The surgeon notes that the tunica vaginalis covers the whole testis and epididymis, so the testis hangs freely within it. What is this anatomical variant called?
questions.e: In the bell-clapper deformity the tunica vaginalis attaches high on the spermatic cord, leaving the testis free to rotate, which predisposes to intravaginal torsion. It is often bilateral, which is why the other testis is fixed at the same operation.

questions.s: A 9-year-old boy has had pain in the right side of the scrotum for 1 day. He is not vomiting. The testis has a normal lie and the cremasteric reflex is present. There is a small tender nodule at the upper pole of the testis that appears as a blue dot through the scrotal skin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A tender nodule at the upper pole with a blue dot sign, a normal lie and a preserved cremasteric reflex in a prepubertal boy is typical of torsion of the appendix testis, which can be managed with analgesia if the diagnosis is certain. Testicular torsion causes diffuse testicular tenderness, an abnormal lie and usually loss of the cremasteric reflex.

questions.s: A 16-year-old is explored for left testicular torsion 4 hours after onset. After untwisting, the testis turns pink and bleeds from a small incision in the tunica albuginea. Besides fixing the left testis, what should be done at the same operation?
questions.e: The anatomical predisposition to torsion (bell-clapper deformity) is usually bilateral, so the contralateral testis is fixed at the same operation. Testicular biopsy and epididymectomy have no role in torsion.

questions.s: A 17-year-old presents to a THQ hospital 30 hours after the onset of right testicular pain. At exploration the testis is black and does not change colour after detorsion and warming for 10 minutes. What is the most appropriate operation?
o: Detorsion and fixation of the right testis only
Right orchidectomy and fixation of the left testis
questions.e: A non-viable testis is removed to prevent infection and possible effects on the other testis, and the contralateral testis is fixed because the predisposing anomaly is usually bilateral. Leaving a dead testis in place risks abscess formation and atrophy.

questions.s: A 14-year-old boy is brought to a rural BHU with sudden testicular pain. The medical officer suspects torsion and arranges urgent referral. Which factor most determines whether the testis can be saved?
o: The time from onset of pain to detorsion
questions.e: Testicular salvage depends mainly on the duration of ischaemia: most testes are saved if detorsion occurs within about 6 hours, and salvage falls sharply after 12 hours. This is why referral and exploration should not be delayed for investigations.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man has a painless left scrotal swelling that has slowly enlarged over a year. It is fluctuant, transilluminates brightly, and the examiner can get above it. The testis cannot be felt separately. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A transilluminating scrotal swelling that one can get above and in which the testis cannot be felt separately is a hydrocele, because fluid surrounds the testis within the tunica vaginalis. An epididymal cyst also transilluminates but lies above and separate from the testis, which remains palpable.

questions.s: A 26-year-old man has developed a tense right hydrocele over 2 months. The testis cannot be palpated clearly through the fluid. He has no pain or fever. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Hydrocele repair by eversion of the sac
questions.e: A new hydrocele in a young man may be secondary to a testicular tumour, and when the testis cannot be felt an ultrasound is needed to assess it. Aspiration or surgery before imaging risks missing a tumour, and scrotal interference could spread it.

questions.s: An 18-year-old has a left scrotal swelling that feels like a bag of worms when he stands and disappears when he lies down. Why does this condition occur more often on the left?
o: The left vein joins the left renal vein at a right angle
The left testicular artery arises from the left renal artery
The left testis hangs lower than the right
The left testicular vein has more valves than the right
questions.e: The left testicular vein enters the left renal vein at a right angle, giving higher pressure and slower drainage, while the right vein enters the inferior vena cava obliquely. The left renal vein can also be compressed between the aorta and superior mesenteric artery, further raising pressure.

questions.s: A 56-year-old man has noticed a right-sided scrotal swelling over 6 weeks. It feels like a bag of worms and does not decompress when he lies flat. He also reports intermittent haematuria. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: Ultrasound of the kidneys and abdomen
questions.e: A new varicocele in an older man, especially on the right or one that does not empty when lying down, suggests venous obstruction by a retroperitoneal or renal mass, such as renal cell carcinoma with tumour thrombus. The abdomen and kidneys must be imaged; scrotal imaging alone would miss the cause.

questions.s: Faraz, 24, has had a painful swollen right testis for 2 days with dysuria and a slight urethral discharge. The epididymis is tender and lifting the testis eases the pain. Doppler shows increased blood flow. Swabs are sent. What is the most appropriate empirical treatment?
o: Oral amoxicillin–clavulanic acid for 14 days with scrotal support
Ceftriaxone single dose plus doxycycline for 10–14 days
questions.e: In a sexually active young man, epididymo-orchitis is usually caused by Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae, so ceftriaxone plus doxycycline is used to cover both. Amoxicillin and nitrofurantoin do not cover these organisms adequately and nitrofurantoin does not reach effective tissue levels.

questions.s: A 67-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia develops fever and a painful, swollen left epididymis and testis a week after a urinary tract infection. He has no new sexual partner. Which organism is the most likely cause?
questions.e: In older men with bladder outflow obstruction or recent urinary infection or instrumentation, epididymo-orchitis is usually caused by enteric organisms such as E. coli. Sexually transmitted organisms are the common cause in younger men, and mumps orchitis mainly affects adolescents and young adults with parotitis.

questions.s: A 28-year-old man has a painless hard lump in the right testis that cannot be separated from it. Ultrasound shows a solid intratesticular mass. Tumour markers are sent. What is the appropriate surgical approach?
o: Radical orchidectomy through an inguinal incision
Orchidectomy through a scrotal incision with cord ligation
questions.e: A solid intratesticular mass is treated as cancer and removed by radical inguinal orchidectomy with high clamping of the cord. Scrotal biopsy or a scrotal incision is avoided because it can spread tumour to scrotal skin and its inguinal lymphatic drainage.

questions.s: A 32-year-old man with a solid testicular mass has a markedly raised serum alpha-fetoprotein and a mildly raised beta-hCG. Which statement about his tumour is correct?
o: It is a pure classical seminoma of the testis
It is a Leydig cell tumour
questions.e: Pure seminomas do not produce alpha-fetoprotein, so a raised AFP indicates a non-seminomatous component such as yolk sac tumour, even if seminoma is also present. A mildly raised hCG can occur in seminoma, so hCG alone does not separate the two.

questions.s: A 58-year-old smoker has painless haematuria and left flank pain. A ballotable mass is felt in the left flank and he has a recent left varicocele. His Hb is 18.2 g/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder
Hydronephrosis from a pelviureteric junction obstruction
questions.e: Haematuria, flank mass, a new left varicocele and polycythaemia in a smoker strongly suggest renal cell carcinoma, which can block the left testicular vein via renal vein tumour thrombus and may secrete erythropoietin. Bladder cancer causes haematuria but not a flank mass or varicocele.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man with von Hippel–Lindau disease is under surveillance. Imaging shows bilateral solid renal masses. What is the most likely histological type of these tumours?
questions.e: Von Hippel–Lindau disease is caused by loss of the VHL tumour suppressor gene on chromosome 3p and predisposes to multiple, bilateral clear cell renal cell carcinomas. Angiomyolipomas are associated with tuberous sclerosis rather than VHL.

questions.s: A 62-year-old woman with a renal cell carcinoma has a serum calcium of 12.6 mg/dL (8.5–10.5) and low PTH. Bone scan shows no metastases. What is the most likely mechanism of her hypercalcaemia?
o: Secretion of PTH-related peptide by the tumour
questions.e: Renal cell carcinoma can cause humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy by secreting PTH-related peptide, which acts on PTH receptors while native PTH is suppressed. Primary hyperparathyroidism would give a raised or inappropriately normal PTH.

questions.s: A mother notices a mass in the abdomen of her 3-year-old son while bathing him. He is well. Examination shows a smooth, firm mass in the right flank that does not cross the midline, BP is raised for age and urine shows microscopic haematuria. Ultrasound shows a solid mass arising from the kidney. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A smooth flank mass arising from the kidney in a well preschool child, with hypertension and haematuria, is typical of Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma). Neuroblastoma arises from the adrenal or sympathetic chain, often crosses the midline, calcifies and usually presents in a sicker child.

questions.s: Ultrasound in a 55-year-old man with haematuria shows a 6 cm solid mass in the upper pole of the left kidney. Which investigation is most appropriate to characterise and stage it?
o: Percutaneous image-guided core biopsy of the renal mass
Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis
questions.e: Contrast-enhanced CT characterises an enhancing renal mass and stages it, including the renal vein, IVC, nodes, adrenals and lungs. Biopsy is not routine because imaging is usually diagnostic, and a bone scan is only needed when there are bone symptoms or a raised alkaline phosphatase.

questions.s: A 52-year-old woman has an incidental 3 cm enhancing solid mass in the lower pole of the right kidney on CT, with no spread. Her other kidney and renal function are normal. What is the preferred treatment?
questions.e: Small localised renal tumours (under 4 cm) are best treated with nephron-sparing partial nephrectomy, which controls the cancer as well as radical surgery while preserving renal function. Renal cell carcinoma responds poorly to conventional chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

questions.s: Muhammad Iqbal, 63, a smoker of 40 pack-years, has had two episodes of painless visible haematuria. Urine culture is negative. Ultrasound of the kidneys is normal. Which investigation is essential next?
questions.e: Painless visible haematuria in a smoker over 45 must be investigated for bladder cancer, and cystoscopy is the key test because ultrasound misses many bladder tumours. Urine cytology is an adjunct with low sensitivity for low-grade tumours and cannot replace cystoscopy.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man has transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder. He has never smoked. Which previous occupation most likely contributed?
o: Work in a textile dye factory
Work in a cotton ginning mill
questions.e: Aromatic amines such as beta-naphthylamine and benzidine, used in the dye, rubber and leather industries, are excreted in urine and cause urothelial carcinoma. Asbestos causes mesothelioma and lung cancer, and cotton dust causes byssinosis.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man who grew up near irrigation canals in a region where Schistosoma haematobium is endemic has haematuria and a bladder mass. Biopsy shows a malignant tumour with keratin pearls. What is the tumour type?
questions.e: Chronic irritation from schistosomal eggs causes squamous metaplasia of the bladder and squamous cell carcinoma, recognised by keratin pearls. Transitional cell carcinoma is the commonest bladder cancer overall, but keratin pearls point to squamous differentiation.

questions.s: A 66-year-old man undergoes transurethral resection of a bladder tumour. Histology shows high-grade urothelial carcinoma invading the lamina propria but not the muscularis propria (pT1), with muscle present in the specimen. What is the most appropriate adjuvant treatment after re-resection?
o: Radical cystectomy for all such patients
questions.e: High-grade non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer has a high risk of recurrence and progression, and intravesical BCG immunotherapy reduces both. Radical cystectomy is considered when BCG fails or in very high-risk disease, while systemic chemotherapy is used for muscle-invasive or metastatic disease.

questions.s: A fit 60-year-old woman has urothelial carcinoma of the bladder invading the muscularis propria, with no nodal or distant spread on CT. What is the standard curative treatment?
o: Radical cystectomy, ideally after neoadjuvant chemotherapy
Intravesical BCG instillations for six weeks then maintenance
questions.e: Muscle-invasive bladder cancer needs radical treatment, standardly radical cystectomy with urinary diversion, with cisplatin-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy improving survival. Intravesical therapies only reach superficial disease and are not adequate once the muscle is invaded.

questions.s: A 74-year-old man with prostate cancer and painful vertebral metastases is to start a long-acting LHRH agonist. Which drug should be started before and with the first injection to prevent tumour flare?
questions.e: LHRH agonists cause an initial surge of LH and testosterone that can worsen bone pain or cause cord compression, so an anti-androgen such as bicalutamide is given to block this flare. Finasteride and tamsulosin treat benign enlargement and do not prevent the flare.

questions.s: A 71-year-old man has low back pain and weight loss. X-ray of the lumbar spine shows multiple dense, sclerotic lesions in the vertebral bodies. Alkaline phosphatase is raised. Which primary tumour is most likely?
questions.e: Prostate cancer characteristically causes osteoblastic (sclerotic) bone metastases in men. Renal and thyroid metastases and myeloma deposits are typically lytic, and myeloma usually has a normal alkaline phosphatase.

questions.s: A 44-year-old woman has her third calcium-containing renal stone. Serum calcium is 11.4 mg/dL (8.5–10.5) and phosphate is low. Which investigation is most appropriate next?
questions.e: Recurrent calcium stones with hypercalcaemia and low phosphate suggest primary hyperparathyroidism, confirmed by a raised or inappropriately normal PTH. Urinary oxalate is part of a stone work-up but would not explain the high serum calcium.

questions.s: A 29-year-old woman has a 9 mm stone in the lower pole of the right kidney causing intermittent pain. A routine test before planned extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy shows she is 8 weeks pregnant. Why is lithotripsy now unsuitable?
o: Pregnancy is a contraindication to shock wave lithotripsy
The stone is too large for shock wave lithotripsy
Lower pole stones cannot be treated by lithotripsy
questions.e: Pregnancy is an absolute contraindication to shock wave lithotripsy because of the risk to the fetus from shock waves and radiation used for targeting. A 9 mm stone is well within the size range for lithotripsy, and lower pole stones can be treated, though clearance is lower.

questions.s: A 47-year-old man has right renal colic. Plain X-ray KUB shows no opacity, but non-contrast CT shows a 6 mm stone at the right vesicoureteric junction. Which stone type is most likely?
questions.e: Pure uric acid stones are radiolucent on plain X-ray but visible on CT. Calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate stones are radio-opaque, and struvite stones are usually visible too.

questions.s: Finasteride is prescribed for a man with a large benign prostate. What is its mechanism of action?
o: Blockade of alpha-1 adrenoceptors in prostatic smooth muscle
Inhibition of conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone
Blockade of androgen receptors in prostatic tissue
questions.e: Finasteride inhibits 5-alpha reductase type 2, reducing dihydrotestosterone, the main androgen driving prostatic growth, so the gland shrinks over months. Alpha-1 blockade is the action of tamsulosin, and androgen receptor blockade is that of anti-androgens such as bicalutamide.

questions.s: A 66-year-old man with benign prostatic enlargement has improved stream on tamsulosin but still has urgency and frequency. Post-void residual volume is 40 mL and urine is clear. Which drug is most appropriate to add?
questions.e: Persistent storage symptoms with a low residual volume can be treated by adding an antimuscarinic such as solifenacin, which reduces detrusor overactivity. A low residual volume is checked first because antimuscarinics can precipitate retention; bethanechol increases detrusor contraction and is not used for urgency.

questions.s: A 76-year-old man with years of untreated prostatic obstruction undergoes cystoscopy. Which bladder finding is a result of long-standing outflow obstruction?
questions.e: Chronic outflow obstruction causes detrusor hypertrophy, seen as trabeculation, with mucosal herniation between muscle bundles forming saccules and diverticula. A smooth thin-walled bladder is the opposite picture, seen in a chronically underactive detrusor.

questions.s: An 84-year-old woman in a care home has abdominal discomfort, overflow incontinence and a palpable bladder. She has had no bowel movement for 8 days and takes codeine for arthritis. What is the most likely cause of her urinary retention?
questions.e: Faecal impaction is a common, reversible cause of urinary retention in elderly patients, especially those taking opioids, because the loaded rectum compresses the bladder neck. A rectal examination confirms it, and treating the constipation often restores voiding.

questions.s: A 70-year-old uncircumcised man had a urethral catheter inserted 2 days ago. The nurse finds his glans swollen and painful, with a tight band of retracted foreskin behind it. What is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Manual reduction of the foreskin after analgesia and compression
Topical steroid cream for one week
questions.e: Paraphimosis occurs when a retracted foreskin is not replaced, for example after catheterisation, and it is treated by reducing the foreskin with analgesia and compression of the oedematous glans. A dorsal slit or circumcision is for failed reduction, and delay risks ischaemia of the glans.

questions.s: A newborn boy is noted at the first check to have a firm, non-tender, dark swelling of the left hemiscrotum that does not transilluminate. He feeds well and is otherwise healthy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Perinatal torsion is extravaginal, with the whole cord and tunica twisting before the tunica is fixed, and presents as a firm, discoloured, painless scrotal mass. A hydrocele would transilluminate, and an incarcerated hernia usually causes distress and vomiting.

questions.s: A 13-year-old with testicular torsion first complains of pain around the umbilicus before the scrotal pain becomes obvious. From which spinal segment does the testis receive its sensory sympathetic innervation that explains this?
questions.e: The testis develops near the kidney and keeps its sympathetic sensory supply from about T10, the same dermatome as the umbilicus, so early testicular pain may be felt periumbilically. This is why scrotal examination is mandatory in a boy with abdominal pain.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man has a smooth, painless swelling in the scrotum. It lies above and behind the testis, which is felt separately, and it transilluminates brightly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An epididymal cyst is a fluid-filled swelling arising from the epididymis, so it transilluminates and lies separate from, above and behind the testis. A hydrocele also transilluminates but surrounds the testis, which then cannot be felt separately.

questions.s: A 35-year-old labourer has a right scrotal swelling that enlarges when he lifts loads. The examiner cannot get above the swelling, it has a cough impulse, and it does not transilluminate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Inability to get above a scrotal swelling means it extends from the inguinal canal, and with a cough impulse this indicates an inguinoscrotal hernia. A hydrocele is confined to the scrotum, so the examiner can get above it, and it transilluminates.

questions.s: A 2-year-old girl has absent irises in both eyes, developmental delay and a renal mass. Deletion on which chromosome links her features?
questions.e: WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumour, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, intellectual disability) is caused by a deletion at 11p13 involving the WT1 and PAX6 genes. Chromosome 13q14 contains the retinoblastoma gene and 22q11 deletion causes DiGeorge syndrome.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man with a large right renal mass develops bilateral leg oedema and dilated veins over the abdominal wall. Which vessel is most likely invaded by tumour thrombus?
questions.e: Renal cell carcinoma tends to grow into the renal vein and can extend as tumour thrombus into the inferior vena cava, causing bilateral leg oedema and abdominal wall collateral veins. Portal vein obstruction causes portal hypertension and ascites rather than leg oedema.

questions.s: Which modifiable risk factor accounts for the largest share of urothelial bladder cancer worldwide?
questions.e: Cigarette smoking is the most important risk factor for urothelial cancer, roughly tripling the risk, because carcinogens excreted in urine bathe the urothelium. Long-term catheterisation is linked mainly to squamous cell carcinoma and affects far fewer people.

questions.s: Zubaida, 67, slips in her courtyard and falls on her outstretched hand. Her wrist looks like a dinner fork from the side. X-ray shows a transverse fracture of the distal radius about 2 cm above the joint with dorsal displacement and dorsal angulation of the distal fragment. What is this fracture called?
questions.e: A Colles fracture is an extra-articular distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement and angulation, typically in an osteoporotic woman after a fall on the outstretched hand, producing the dinner-fork deformity. A Smith fracture has volar displacement, usually after a fall on the flexed wrist.

questions.s: A 22-year-old cricketer falls on his outstretched hand. He has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox and pain on axial compression of the thumb. Scaphoid-view X-rays show no fracture. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Crepe bandage and review if pain persists after 6 weeks
Immobilise in a splint and arrange MRI or repeat X-rays in 10–14 days
Immediate open reduction and internal fixation with a compression screw
questions.e: Scaphoid fractures are often invisible on initial X-rays, so clinical suspicion is treated as a fracture with immobilisation and further imaging (MRI, CT or repeat films). A missed scaphoid fracture can progress to non-union or avascular necrosis of the proximal pole, so discharge without follow-up is unsafe.

questions.s: A 7-year-old boy falls from a tree onto his outstretched arm and sustains a displaced extension-type supracondylar fracture of the humerus. The hand is warm and pink. He cannot flex the tip of his thumb or index finger to make an 'OK' sign, but sensation in the hand is normal. Which nerve is injured?
questions.e: The anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve supplies flexor pollicis longus and the lateral flexor digitorum profundus, so injury prevents the 'OK' sign with no sensory loss because the nerve is purely motor. It is the nerve most often injured in extension-type supracondylar fractures; radial nerve injury would cause weak wrist and finger extension.

questions.s: An 8-year-old with a displaced supracondylar fracture of the humerus has a cold, pale hand with no radial pulse before reduction. Which artery is most at risk in this injury?
questions.e: The sharp proximal fragment of an extension supracondylar fracture is displaced anteriorly and can kink, compress or tear the brachial artery in the cubital fossa. Untreated ischaemia can lead to forearm compartment syndrome and Volkmann ischaemic contracture, so a pulseless hand needs urgent reduction.

questions.s: A 24-year-old kabaddi player falls on his abducted, externally rotated arm. His shoulder has lost its rounded contour and the humeral head is palpable in front. Before attempting reduction, sensation over which area must be tested and documented?
o: The tip of the little finger
The lateral aspect of the upper arm over the deltoid
The dorsal web space between the thumb and the index finger
The medial aspect of the forearm
questions.e: Anterior shoulder dislocation can stretch the axillary nerve, which supplies the deltoid and the skin over its lower half (the regimental badge area). Sensation there is checked and recorded before and after reduction; the dorsal first web space is supplied by the radial nerve.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man is brought in after a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. He holds his right arm internally rotated and adducted and cannot externally rotate it. AP X-ray shows a symmetrical 'light bulb' appearance of the humeral head. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Posterior dislocation is classically caused by seizures or electric shock, when strong internal rotators overpower the external rotators; the arm is locked in internal rotation and the humeral head looks like a light bulb on AP view. It is easily missed on a single AP film, so a lateral or axillary view is needed.

questions.s: A 19-year-old falls off a motorbike onto his shoulder. X-ray shows a minimally displaced fracture of the middle third of the right clavicle. Skin is intact and the arm is neurovascularly normal. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Figure-of-eight bandage applied tightly for 12 weeks
questions.e: Most minimally displaced midshaft clavicle fractures heal well with a broad arm sling, analgesia and early movement as pain allows. Surgery is reserved for open fractures, skin tenting, neurovascular injury or marked displacement and shortening.

questions.s: A 28-year-old man raises his forearm to block a stick blow. X-ray shows a fracture of the proximal third of the ulnar shaft. The radial head does not line up with the capitulum on the lateral view. What is this injury called?
questions.e: A proximal ulnar fracture with dislocation of the radial head is a Monteggia injury; a line through the radial neck should always pass through the capitulum, and the elbow must be imaged with every forearm fracture. Galeazzi is the opposite pattern: a distal radial shaft fracture with distal radioulnar joint dislocation.

questions.s: A 3-year-old girl started crying and refused to use her left arm after her father pulled her up by the hand onto a bus. She holds the arm slightly flexed and pronated. There is no swelling or bruising. What is the most appropriate management?
o: X-ray of the elbow, then an above-elbow plaster cast
Supination and flexion of the forearm
questions.e: A pulled elbow is subluxation of the radial head under the annular ligament after traction on the extended, pronated arm. It is reduced by supination and flexion or by hyperpronation, often with a click, and the child soon uses the arm again; X-rays are not needed with a typical history and normal examination.

questions.s: A 21-year-old man punched a wall in anger. The knuckle of his right little finger is depressed and the dorsum of the hand is swollen. Which bone is most likely fractured?
o: Shaft of the proximal phalanx of the little finger
questions.e: Punching a hard object typically fractures the neck of the fifth metacarpal (boxer's fracture), giving a depressed knuckle. A wound over the knuckle from a punch to the mouth must be treated as a human bite; a fracture at the base of the first metacarpal is a Bennett fracture.

questions.s: A 78-year-old woman with osteoporosis falls and sustains a minimally displaced fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus. Neurovascular examination is normal. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Open reduction and locking plate fixation
Collar and cuff sling with early mobilisation
questions.e: Most minimally displaced proximal humerus fractures in older people are treated in a sling with early gentle mobilisation to avoid stiffness. Surgery is considered for markedly displaced fractures, fracture-dislocations and some head-splitting injuries.

questions.s: A 35-year-old carpenter injures his hand. X-ray shows an intra-articular fracture at the base of the first metacarpal, with a small medial fragment staying attached and the shaft pulled proximally and radially. Which muscle mainly causes the displacement of the shaft?
questions.e: In a Bennett fracture the small volar-ulnar fragment is held by the ligament while abductor pollicis longus, inserted into the base of the first metacarpal, pulls the shaft proximally and radially. This unstable intra-articular fracture usually needs fixation.

questions.s: Rehmat Bibi, 84, walks indoors only with a frame and has moderate dementia. After a fall her left leg is shortened and externally rotated. X-ray shows a displaced intracapsular fracture of the femoral neck. She is otherwise fit for surgery. What is the most appropriate operation?
questions.e: Displaced intracapsular fractures disrupt the blood supply of the femoral head, so the head is replaced rather than fixed; hemiarthroplasty suits older patients with limited mobility or cognitive impairment. Total hip replacement is offered to fit, independently mobile patients, and screw fixation is used for undisplaced fractures.

questions.s: A 79-year-old man falls at home. X-ray shows a stable two-part intertrochanteric fracture of the right femur. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Extracapsular fractures leave the blood supply of the femoral head intact, so the fracture is fixed; a sliding hip screw is standard for stable intertrochanteric fractures. Replacement is for displaced intracapsular fractures, and prolonged traction carries high risk of pressure sores, pneumonia and thrombosis.

questions.s: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head is a common complication of displaced intracapsular femoral neck fractures. Which artery provides most of the blood supply to the adult femoral head?
questions.e: In adults the femoral head is supplied mainly by retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery that run along the neck, and these are torn in displaced intracapsular fractures. The artery of the ligamentum teres contributes little after childhood.

questions.s: A 32-year-old car passenger hits his knee against the dashboard in a collision on the motorway. His right leg is shortened, flexed, adducted and internally rotated at the hip. Which nerve is most at risk?
questions.e: A dashboard injury drives the femoral head backwards, causing posterior hip dislocation with the limb flexed, adducted and internally rotated, and the sciatic nerve lying behind the joint can be stretched. Urgent reduction is needed to reduce the risk of avascular necrosis and nerve damage.

questions.s: A 23-year-old man with a closed femoral shaft fracture awaiting fixation becomes confused 36 hours after injury. RR is 30/min, SpO₂ 86 % on air, and there are petechiae over his chest, axillae and conjunctivae. Chest X-ray shows bilateral patchy shadowing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: The triad of respiratory distress, neurological change and petechial rash 24–72 hours after a long-bone fracture is typical of fat embolism syndrome. Pulmonary embolism does not cause a petechial rash, and early fracture fixation reduces the risk of fat embolism.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man arrives at the emergency department with an open fracture of the tibial shaft after a motorbike accident. There is a 3 cm wound with bone visible. He is haemodynamically stable. Apart from analgesia, splinting and tetanus cover, which step should be done first in the emergency department?
o: Primary closure of the wound in the emergency department
Intravenous antibiotics as soon as possible
Immediate internal fixation in the emergency department
Wound swab culture before giving any antibiotic
questions.e: In open fractures, early intravenous antibiotics, ideally within an hour, are the most important measure to reduce deep infection, along with photographing and covering the wound with a saline dressing. Formal debridement and stabilisation follow in theatre; primary closure in the emergency room and swab-guided delay are harmful.

questions.s: A 26-year-old woman twists her ankle walking on an uneven pavement. She has swelling over the lateral ankle. According to the Ottawa ankle rules, which finding means she needs an ankle X-ray?
o: Marked swelling and pain below the lateral malleolus on standing
Pain on inversion of the foot
Bone tenderness at the posterior edge of the lateral malleolus
questions.e: Ankle X-ray is indicated if there is malleolar pain with bone tenderness along the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, or inability to bear weight for four steps both immediately and in the department. Swelling and bruising alone are common in ligament sprains and do not mandate imaging.

questions.s: A 40-year-old woman has an ankle injury. X-ray shows a fracture of the fibula above the syndesmosis with widening of the medial clear space, indicating talar shift. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Compression bandage and early weight bearing
questions.e: A Weber C fibular fracture with talar shift is unstable because the syndesmosis and medial structures are disrupted; open reduction and internal fixation restores the mortise and prevents early arthritis. Cast or brace treatment is for stable injuries without talar shift.

questions.s: A 22-year-old footballer lands awkwardly while pivoting and feels a 'pop' in his knee. The knee swells within 1 hour. A few days later, the tibia moves forward excessively on the femur with the knee flexed 20–30°. What is the most likely injury?
questions.e: A non-contact pivoting injury with a pop, rapid haemarthrosis and a positive Lachman test is typical of an anterior cruciate ligament tear. Meniscal tears usually swell more slowly, over hours to a day, and cause locking or joint-line tenderness.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man twisted his knee while squatting. The knee swelled the next day and he now has medial joint-line tenderness and episodes when the knee 'locks' and he cannot fully straighten it. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Twisting on a flexed knee, delayed swelling, joint-line tenderness and true locking point to a meniscal tear, with a displaced fragment blocking extension. A medial collateral ligament sprain causes tenderness along the ligament and pain on valgus stress, but not locking.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man playing badminton feels as if someone kicked the back of his ankle. He can walk with a limp. Lying prone, squeezing his calf does not cause plantarflexion of the foot, and a gap is felt above the heel. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A sudden 'kick' sensation, a palpable gap and absent plantarflexion on calf squeeze (Simmonds or Thompson test) indicate Achilles tendon rupture. Patients may still walk and weakly plantarflex using the long toe flexors, so this is easily missed.

questions.s: Usman, an overweight 13-year-old boy, has had a limp and left knee pain for 4 weeks. Knee examination is normal. Hip flexion is accompanied by obligatory external rotation and internal rotation is reduced. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Transient synovitis of the hip joint
questions.e: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis typically affects overweight adolescents, may present with referred knee pain, and causes loss of internal rotation with external rotation on flexion; a frog-leg lateral X-ray shows the slip. Perthes disease affects younger children, usually 4–8 years old.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man had a closed tibial shaft fracture treated in an above-knee plaster 8 hours ago. He now has severe pain not relieved by morphine and pain when his toes are passively extended. Foot pulses are palpable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretch of the muscles are the earliest signs of compartment syndrome. Pulses usually remain present because compartment pressure rarely exceeds arterial pressure, so a palpable pulse does not exclude it.

questions.s: A 28-year-old man with a tibial fracture in a full plaster cast has increasing leg pain and pain on passive toe movement. The cast and padding are split down to the skin and the leg is placed at heart level, but 30 minutes later his pain and signs are unchanged. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Elevate the leg above heart level and give more opioid
Emergency fasciotomy of all four leg compartments
Doppler ultrasound of the leg veins
questions.e: Clinical compartment syndrome that persists after all dressings are released down to skin requires urgent fasciotomy of all compartments to prevent muscle and nerve necrosis. Elevation above heart level reduces arterial inflow and worsens perfusion, and waiting allows irreversible damage.

questions.s: Junior doctors on an orthopaedic ward in Multan are taught to look for compartment syndrome after forearm and leg fractures. Which is the earliest and most reliable clinical sign?
o: Absent distal pulses on palpation and on Doppler examination
Pain on passive stretch of the compartment muscles
