questions.e: Pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretch are the earliest signs of raised compartment pressure. Pulselessness, pallor and paralysis are late findings that indicate established ischaemia, and waiting for them leads to permanent damage.

questions.s: A sedated, ventilated 35-year-old with a tibial plateau fracture cannot report pain. Compartment pressures are measured. His diastolic BP is 60 mmHg and the anterior compartment pressure is 42 mmHg. What is the best interpretation?
o: Normal compartment pressure; repeat the measurement in 12 hours
A perfusion gradient of 18 mmHg indicates the need for fasciotomy
Compartment syndrome only if pressure exceeds diastolic pressure
Raised pressure but fasciotomy is only needed if pulses are lost
questions.e: A perfusion gradient (diastolic pressure minus compartment pressure) below 30 mmHg indicates inadequate tissue perfusion and is the usual threshold for fasciotomy. Waiting for loss of pulses or for compartment pressure to exceed diastolic pressure would allow muscle necrosis.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man was trapped under a collapsed wall in an earthquake for 10 hours. After release his right thigh and leg are tense and swollen. His urine is dark brown, dipstick positive for blood, but microscopy shows no red cells. CK is 45,000 U/L. Which immediate treatment best protects his kidneys?
o: Intravenous furosemide to force a high urine output
questions.e: Crush injury causes rhabdomyolysis, and myoglobin produces dark urine positive for blood on dipstick without red cells; aggressive intravenous isotonic fluid to maintain high urine output reduces myoglobin-induced acute kidney injury. Furosemide may worsen hypovolaemia, and dialysis is used only for refractory AKI, hyperkalaemia or overload.

questions.s: Ali, a 6-year-old boy, has had fever and severe pain above the right knee for 3 days and refuses to walk. The distal femur is warm and very tender. CRP is high. Which organism is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest cause of acute haematogenous osteomyelitis at all ages, typically affecting the metaphysis of long bones in children. Pseudomonas is linked to puncture wounds through shoes, and Salmonella is classically associated with sickle cell disease.

questions.s: A 9-year-old boy with sickle cell anaemia has fever and pain in the left tibia for a week, not improving with treatment for a vaso-occlusive crisis. MRI confirms osteomyelitis. Besides Staphylococcus aureus, which organism must the empirical antibiotics cover?
questions.e: Patients with sickle cell disease are particularly prone to Salmonella osteomyelitis, related to bowel infarcts allowing bacterial entry and to splenic dysfunction. Empirical therapy should therefore cover Salmonella as well as S. aureus, for example with a third-generation cephalosporin.

questions.s: Acute haematogenous osteomyelitis in children usually starts in the metaphysis of long bones. What explains this site?
o: Slow, turbulent flow in metaphyseal capillary loops
The epiphysis has an end-arterial supply from the joint capsule
The diaphysis has the richest blood supply
questions.e: Metaphyseal capillaries form hairpin loops with slow, turbulent flow and few phagocytes, so circulating bacteria settle there. The growth plate then acts as a barrier that limits spread into the epiphysis in older children.

questions.s: Sana, a 4-year-old girl, has had fever of 39.2 °C and refused to bear weight on her right leg for 2 days. She holds the hip flexed, abducted and externally rotated, and any movement is very painful. WBC is 18,000/mm³ and CRP 110 mg/L. Ultrasound shows a hip effusion. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Oral ibuprofen and review in 48 hours
Urgent aspiration of the hip joint
MRI of the pelvis under sedation
questions.e: Fever, inability to bear weight, high WBC and CRP and an effusion make septic arthritis likely, so the hip is aspirated urgently for Gram stain and culture, followed by washout and intravenous antibiotics. Pus in a joint quickly destroys cartilage and can cause avascular necrosis of the femoral head, so delay for observation or MRI is unsafe.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man has had a discharging sinus over his left tibia for 2 years after an open fracture. X-ray shows a dense, separated fragment of bone surrounded by a lucent zone and a shell of new periosteal bone. What is the definitive treatment?
o: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy with long-term antibiotics
Removal of dead bone, debridement and antibiotics
questions.e: Chronic osteomyelitis with a sequestrum (a separated fragment of dead bone) cannot be cured by antibiotics alone because dead bone has no blood supply; sequestrectomy and debridement with targeted antibiotics are needed. Amputation is a last resort for uncontrollable infection or a non-functional limb.

questions.s: A 14-year-old boy has had a dull ache in the upper tibia for 3 months, worse at night. He is afebrile and inflammatory markers are mildly raised. X-ray shows a well-defined lucent lesion in the proximal tibial metaphysis with a thick sclerotic rim. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A Brodie abscess is a localised subacute osteomyelitis in which host defences wall off the infection, producing a metaphyseal lucency with a sclerotic rim and chronic pain without systemic upset. Osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma show aggressive, poorly defined destruction with periosteal reaction.

questions.s: Shazia, 32, from rural Punjab has had back pain for 4 months with evening fever and weight loss. There is a small angular kyphosis at the thoracolumbar junction. X-ray shows destruction of the adjacent margins of T12 and L1 with loss of the disc space between them and a fusiform paravertebral shadow. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Constitutional symptoms with a gibbus and destruction of two adjacent vertebrae with loss of the intervening disc and a paravertebral abscess are typical of spinal tuberculosis (Pott disease). Metastases usually destroy the pedicles and vertebral bodies but spare the disc space.

questions.s: A 55-year-old diabetic man has a hot, swollen, painful right knee with fever for 2 days. Knee aspiration yields turbid fluid with 85,000 white cells/mm³, mostly neutrophils, and Gram-positive cocci in clusters. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Rest, NSAIDs and repeat aspiration in 1 week
questions.e: Purulent synovial fluid with Gram-positive cocci in clusters indicates staphylococcal septic arthritis, treated by drainage (arthroscopic or open washout, or repeated aspiration) plus intravenous antibiotics. Steroid injection into an infected joint is dangerous, and colchicine treats gout, which shows crystals rather than bacteria.

questions.s: A 15-year-old boy has had increasing pain and swelling above the left knee for 2 months, waking him at night. X-ray of the distal femoral metaphysis shows a destructive lesion with a 'sunburst' periosteal reaction and a Codman triangle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Osteosarcoma is the commonest primary malignant bone tumour in adolescents, usually around the knee in the metaphysis, with sunburst spiculation and a Codman triangle from lifted periosteum. Ewing sarcoma tends to affect the diaphysis and gives an onion-skin periosteal reaction.

questions.s: A 12-year-old girl has a painful swelling in the middle of her right femur, intermittent fever and a raised ESR. X-ray shows a permeative lesion in the diaphysis with a layered 'onion-skin' periosteal reaction. Biopsy shows sheets of small round blue cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Ewing sarcoma affects children and adolescents, involves the diaphysis, gives an onion-skin periosteal reaction and is composed of small round blue cells; fever and raised ESR can mimic infection. Osteomyelitis is in the differential, but biopsy showing small round blue cells settles the diagnosis.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman has a painful swelling at the knee. X-ray shows an eccentric, expansile lytic lesion with a 'soap-bubble' appearance in the distal femoral epiphysis, extending to the subchondral bone. Her growth plates are closed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Giant cell tumour typically occurs after skeletal maturity, in the epiphysis of a long bone around the knee, as an eccentric expansile lytic lesion reaching the subchondral bone. Aneurysmal bone cysts and simple bone cysts usually occur in the metaphysis of younger patients.

questions.s: A 19-year-old man has had pain in his left thigh for 6 months, worse at night and relieved promptly by NSAIDs. CT shows a small lucent nidus under 1.5 cm in the femoral cortex surrounded by dense sclerosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Osteoid osteoma is a benign tumour of young people producing prostaglandins that cause night pain relieved by NSAIDs; imaging shows a small nidus with surrounding reactive sclerosis. It is commonly treated by radiofrequency ablation if symptoms persist.

questions.s: A 16-year-old boy has a painless hard lump near his knee that has been present for years. X-ray shows a bony projection from the metaphysis of the distal femur pointing away from the joint, with its cortex and medulla continuous with the parent bone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Osteochondroma, the commonest benign bone tumour, is a cartilage-capped bony outgrowth from the metaphysis that points away from the joint and shares cortex and medulla with the parent bone. Enchondromas lie within the medulla, often in the small bones of the hand.

questions.s: A 66-year-old man has back pain, anaemia, raised creatinine and multiple 'punched-out' lytic lesions in the skull on X-ray. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal band. Which investigation is least sensitive for detecting his bone lesions?
questions.e: Myeloma lesions are purely lytic with little osteoblastic activity, so isotope bone scans are often normal ('cold'). Whole-body low-dose CT and MRI are the most sensitive, and a skeletal survey still detects established lytic lesions.

questions.s: A 55-year-old woman with known breast cancer has pain in the right thigh on walking. X-ray shows a lytic metastasis in the subtrochanteric femur destroying more than half of the cortical thickness. There is no fracture. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Prophylactic intramedullary nailing followed by radiotherapy
Radiotherapy alone with full weight bearing as tolerated
Bisphosphonate infusion and review in 3 months
questions.e: A painful lytic lesion with more than 50 % cortical destruction in the high-stress peritrochanteric region has a high risk of pathological fracture, so prophylactic fixation is followed by radiotherapy to the whole bone. Radiotherapy alone does not restore strength quickly enough to prevent fracture.

questions.s: Saleem, 38, a porter, has low back pain radiating down the back of his left thigh and calf to the sole and lateral border of the foot. The left ankle reflex is absent and plantarflexion is weak. Which nerve root is most likely compressed?
questions.e: S1 root compression, usually from an L5/S1 disc prolapse, causes pain and numbness along the back of the leg to the sole and lateral foot, weak plantarflexion and a reduced ankle reflex. L5 compression weakens great toe extension and ankle dorsiflexion with numbness over the dorsum of the foot, and the reflexes are usually preserved.

questions.s: A 42-year-old woman has sciatica with numbness over the dorsum of the right foot and first web space. She has weakness of great toe extension; knee and ankle reflexes are normal. Which disc prolapse most likely explains this?
questions.e: Weak extensor hallucis longus and numbness over the dorsum of the foot indicate an L5 root lesion, usually caused by a posterolateral L4/L5 disc prolapse compressing the traversing L5 root. An L5/S1 prolapse typically affects S1, reducing the ankle reflex.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man with a 2-week history of sciatica now has pain down both legs, numbness around the anus and perineum, and has not passed urine for 12 hours. Anal tone is reduced. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Urgent MRI of the lumbosacral spine
Plain X-ray of the lumbar spine
Physiotherapy referral and analgesia review in one week
questions.e: Bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention and reduced anal tone indicate cauda equina syndrome, which needs emergency MRI and surgical decompression to preserve bladder, bowel and sexual function. Plain X-rays do not show disc or neural compression.

questions.s: A 33-year-old office worker has had low back pain for 5 days after lifting a heavy box. There is no leg pain, numbness, bladder symptoms, fever, weight loss or history of cancer. Neurological examination is normal. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Strict bed rest on a firm mattress for 2 weeks
Advice to stay active with NSAIDs as needed
questions.e: Acute non-specific low back pain without red flags is managed with reassurance, advice to keep active and simple analgesia such as an NSAID. Imaging does not change management and may find incidental changes, and bed rest delays recovery.

questions.s: A 28-year-old woman wearing only a lap belt is in a head-on car crash. She has a bruise across her lower abdomen and back pain. CT shows a horizontal fracture through the body, pedicles and spinous process of L1 (a flexion-distraction injury). Which associated injury must be actively looked for?
questions.e: A Chance (flexion-distraction) fracture from a lap belt is strongly associated with hollow viscus injury, especially of the small bowel and mesentery, which CT can miss early. Calcaneal fractures are linked with lumbar burst fractures from falls onto the feet, not seat-belt injuries.

questions.s: A 74-year-old man with cervical spondylosis falls forward and hits his forehead, hyperextending his neck. He has marked weakness of both arms and hands, with milder weakness of the legs, and can still pass urine. CT shows no fracture. Which spinal cord syndrome is most likely?
questions.e: Hyperextension in an older person with a narrowed spondylotic canal compresses the central cord, where the arm fibres of the corticospinal tracts lie medially, so the arms are weaker than the legs. Anterior cord syndrome causes paralysis and loss of pain sensation below the lesion with preserved proprioception.

questions.s: A 72-year-old woman falls down three stairs at home and complains of neck pain. She has no neurological deficit. By the Canadian C-spine rule she is high risk because of her age. Which imaging is most appropriate?
o: Three-view plain X-rays of the cervical spine
No imaging if she can rotate her neck 45°
questions.e: Adults at high risk of cervical spine injury, including those aged 65 or over, should have CT of the cervical spine, which is far more sensitive than plain films for fractures. The rotation test is only applied to low-risk patients, and flexion-extension views are unsafe in the acute setting.

questions.s: During a school health check in Islamabad, a 13-year-old girl is noted to have uneven shoulders. Which bedside test best screens for structural scoliosis?
questions.e: In the Adams forward bending test, vertebral rotation in structural scoliosis produces a rib hump that becomes obvious when the child bends forward. The Schober test measures lumbar flexion, used in ankylosing spondylitis, and straight leg raising tests for nerve root tension.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man falls from a motorcycle and sustains a spiral fracture of the middle third of the humeral shaft. He cannot extend his wrist or fingers and has numbness over the dorsum of the first web space. Which nerve is injured?
questions.e: The radial nerve winds around the humerus in the spiral groove and is commonly injured by midshaft fractures, causing wrist drop and numbness over the dorsal first web space. Most cases are neurapraxia and recover with conservative treatment of the fracture.

questions.s: Farah, 30, is 32 weeks pregnant and has tingling of the thumb, index and middle fingers that wakes her at night. Shaking her hand relieves it. Tinel and Phalen tests are positive and there is no muscle wasting. What is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Night-time wrist splint in a neutral position
Nerve conduction studies before any treatment
questions.e: Carpal tunnel syndrome in pregnancy is caused by fluid retention and usually resolves after delivery, so a neutral wrist splint at night is first-line. Surgery is reserved for persistent or severe cases with wasting or weakness, and nerve studies are not needed before conservative treatment of a typical case.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man has a fracture of the medial epicondyle of the humerus. When asked to grip a sheet of paper between his thumb and the side of his index finger, he flexes the thumb at the interphalangeal joint. Which nerve is injured?
questions.e: Froment's sign shows weakness of adductor pollicis, supplied by the ulnar nerve, so the patient substitutes flexor pollicis longus (median nerve) and flexes the thumb tip. The ulnar nerve runs behind the medial epicondyle and is easily injured there.

questions.s: A baby boy weighing 4.6 kg is delivered with shoulder dystocia at a THQ hospital. His right arm hangs by his side, adducted and internally rotated, with the elbow extended and the forearm pronated. The grasp reflex is present. Which roots are injured?
questions.e: Erb palsy results from traction injury to the upper trunk (C5–C6), paralysing the shoulder abductors, external rotators, elbow flexors and supinators, giving the 'waiter's tip' posture with a preserved grasp. Lower root injury (C8–T1, Klumpke palsy) affects the small muscles of the hand.

questions.s: A 20-year-old man grabbed a railing to stop a fall from a height, forcibly abducting his arm. He now has a claw hand with wasting of the small hand muscles, numbness along the inner forearm, and on the same side a small pupil and drooping eyelid. Which injury is most likely?
o: Upper trunk lesion of the brachial plexus
Lower trunk lesion with avulsion of the T1 root
Ulnar nerve injury at the elbow
Radial nerve injury in the axilla
questions.e: Forced abduction injures the lower trunk (C8–T1), causing Klumpke palsy with weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles and medial forearm numbness. An ipsilateral Horner syndrome indicates T1 root avulsion close to the cord, damaging sympathetic fibres to the eye and suggesting a poor prognosis.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man has a fracture of the neck of the fibula after a side impact to the knee. He walks with a high-stepping gait and cannot dorsiflex or evert his foot. Which nerve is injured?
questions.e: The common peroneal (fibular) nerve winds around the neck of the fibula, where fractures or tight plasters can injure it, causing foot drop with loss of dorsiflexion and eversion. Tibial nerve injury weakens plantarflexion and inversion and causes numbness of the sole.

questions.s: A 50-year-old woman has a mastectomy with axillary node clearance. Afterwards the medial border of her scapula sticks out when she pushes against a wall. Which nerve has been damaged?
questions.e: The long thoracic nerve runs on the medial wall of the axilla and supplies serratus anterior, which holds the scapula against the chest wall; damage causes winging of the scapula. The thoracodorsal nerve supplies latissimus dorsi, whose loss weakens adduction and extension rather than causing winging.

questions.s: After a long operation with an upper-arm tourniquet, a 30-year-old man has weakness of wrist extension and patchy numbness. Nerve conduction shows a block at the tourniquet site with normal conduction distal to it. He recovers fully within 4 weeks. What type of nerve injury was this?
questions.e: Neurapraxia is a local conduction block, often from compression, with intact axons, so there is no Wallerian degeneration and recovery is complete within weeks. Axonotmesis involves axonal disruption with distal degeneration and recovery by regrowth at about 1 mm per day.

questions.s: A 24-year-old man had a scaphoid fracture through the waist treated in a cast. Six months later he still has wrist pain. MRI shows the proximal pole is dense with low signal. What is the most likely complication?
o: Avascular necrosis of the proximal pole
questions.e: The scaphoid's blood supply enters distally and flows retrograde, so fractures through the waist or proximal pole can deprive the proximal fragment of blood, causing avascular necrosis and non-union. Malunion of the scaphoid is less common and does not produce a dead proximal pole.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man falls on his hand. X-ray shows a fracture of the distal third of the radial shaft with the ulnar head dislocated at the wrist. What is this injury called?
questions.e: A Galeazzi injury is a distal radial shaft fracture with dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint, and in adults it needs open reduction and fixation. Monteggia is the reverse pattern, with a proximal ulnar fracture and radial head dislocation.

questions.s: A 60-year-old woman falls backwards onto the back of her flexed wrist. X-ray shows a transverse fracture of the distal radius with the distal fragment displaced and angled towards the palm. What is this fracture called?
questions.e: A Smith fracture is a distal radius fracture with volar displacement of the distal fragment, often called a reverse Colles fracture, and is usually unstable. A Colles fracture has dorsal displacement after a fall on the outstretched hand.

questions.s: At her 6-week check, a firstborn girl delivered by breech has a clunk when the flexed and abducted hip is lifted forward (Ortolani test). Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: In infants under about 4–6 months the femoral heads are largely cartilaginous, so ultrasound is the investigation of choice for developmental dysplasia of the hip. Plain X-rays become useful once the femoral head ossific nucleus appears.

questions.s: A 6-year-old boy has had a painless limp for 2 months. He is afebrile, with limited abduction and internal rotation of the right hip. X-ray shows a flattened, sclerotic and fragmented right femoral capital epiphysis. What is the underlying process?
o: Slipped epiphysis at the growth plate
Bacterial infection of the hip joint
Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head
Inflammatory synovitis after a viral infection
questions.e: Perthes disease is idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral capital epiphysis in children, usually boys aged 4–8, presenting with a painless or mildly painful limp and X-ray sclerosis, fragmentation and flattening. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis affects older, often overweight adolescents.

questions.s: A 13-year-old boy who plays football daily has pain below the right kneecap that is worse after running and kneeling. There is a tender bony lump over the tibial tuberosity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Osgood–Schlatter disease is a traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity in active adolescents during growth spurts, causing a tender bony lump, and it settles with activity modification. Osteosarcoma causes progressive, constant and night pain rather than activity-related pain over the tuberosity.

questions.s: A 10-year-old boy had an untreated supracondylar fracture with a pulseless hand 6 months ago. He now has a fixed flexion deformity of the wrist and fingers that worsens when the wrist is extended. Which muscle group is mainly involved?
o: Deep flexor muscles of the forearm
questions.e: Volkmann ischaemic contracture follows untreated forearm compartment syndrome, most often affecting the deep flexors (flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus), which become fibrotic and shortened. The deformity worsens when the wrist is extended because the shortened flexors are stretched.

questions.s: A nurse asks which finding in suspected compartment syndrome of the leg is a late sign, indicating that ischaemic damage is already advanced. Which is it?
o: Pain out of proportion to the injury
questions.e: Loss of distal pulses occurs late, if at all, because compartment pressure rarely exceeds arterial pressure; by then muscle necrosis is usually established. Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are the early warning signs that should prompt action.

questions.s: A 5-year-old boy has had a limp and mild right hip pain for 2 days after a cold last week. He is afebrile, bears some weight, and has mildly reduced internal rotation. WBC and CRP are normal. Ultrasound shows a small hip effusion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Transient synovitis follows a viral infection in young children, causes a limp with mild pain and a small effusion, and the child is afebrile with normal inflammatory markers. Septic arthritis is suggested by fever, refusal to bear weight, raised WBC and high CRP.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man from Quetta has 6 weeks of mid-back pain, night sweats and weight loss. Chest X-ray shows old apical scarring. Which is the earliest radiographic change expected in early tuberculous spondylitis?
o: Narrowing of the disc space with paradiscal erosion
questions.e: Spinal tuberculosis usually begins in the paradiscal region, and the earliest X-ray signs are narrowing of the disc space and erosion of adjacent vertebral margins; collapse and gibbus come later. A bamboo spine is a feature of ankylosing spondylitis.

questions.s: A 42-year-old man has had a known bony lump on his upper humerus since childhood. It has started to enlarge and become painful over 6 months. MRI shows a cartilage cap 3 cm thick. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Growth or new pain in an osteochondroma after skeletal maturity, especially with a cartilage cap thicker than about 2 cm, suggests malignant change to chondrosarcoma. Overlying bursitis can cause pain but does not thicken the cartilage cap.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man has dull pain in the left hip and buttock for a year. X-ray shows a lytic lesion in the ilium with stippled 'rings and arcs' calcification and cortical thickening. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Chondrosarcoma typically affects middle-aged and older adults in the pelvis and proximal long bones, with a chondroid matrix showing rings-and-arcs calcification. Osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma are mainly tumours of children and adolescents.

questions.s: Among patients presenting to a GP clinic with low back pain, which feature most strongly calls for urgent imaging to exclude spinal metastasis?
o: Pain after lifting a heavy object
Previous breast cancer with constant night pain
questions.e: A history of cancer, together with constant or night pain, is a red flag for spinal metastasis and calls for urgent MRI. Pain after lifting or prolonged sitting fits mechanical back pain, and brief morning stiffness is common in non-specific back pain.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man has pain from the front of the thigh to the medial side of the leg, weak knee extension and a reduced knee reflex. Which nerve root is most likely compressed?
questions.e: L4 root compression causes pain over the anterior thigh and medial leg, weak quadriceps and a reduced knee reflex. An L5 lesion spares the knee reflex and weakens great toe extension, and S1 reduces the ankle reflex.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man is stabbed in the back on the right side at the T10 level. He has weakness of the right leg and loss of vibration and joint position sense in the right leg. Which other finding is expected?
o: Loss of pain and temperature sensation in the left leg
Loss of pain and temperature sensation in the right leg
Loss of all sensation in both legs
questions.e: Brown-Séquard syndrome (hemisection of the cord) causes ipsilateral motor weakness and loss of dorsal column sensation, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature because the spinothalamic fibres cross within one or two segments of entry. The opposite leg keeps its power.

questions.s: A 45-year-old obese man who has recently started wearing a tight work belt has burning pain and numbness over the outer front of the right thigh. Power and reflexes are normal. Which nerve is compressed?
o: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
questions.e: Meralgia paraesthetica is entrapment of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh as it passes under or through the inguinal ligament near the anterior superior iliac spine, causing purely sensory symptoms on the anterolateral thigh. An L3 or femoral nerve lesion would reduce knee reflex or power.

questions.s: After fixation of a radial head fracture, a 35-year-old woman cannot extend her fingers at the metacarpophalangeal joints, but she can extend her wrist (with radial deviation) and has no sensory loss. Which nerve is injured?
o: Radial nerve in the spiral groove
questions.e: The posterior interosseous nerve is the deep motor branch of the radial nerve around the radial neck; injury causes finger drop without wrist drop or sensory loss, and the wrist deviates radially because extensor carpi radialis longus is spared. A spiral groove lesion causes wrist drop with numbness over the first dorsal web space.

questions.s: A 6-year-old boy develops foot drop and numbness of the sole after an intramuscular injection given into the lower inner part of the buttock at a private clinic. To avoid this injury, where should a gluteal intramuscular injection be given?
o: Lower inner quadrant of the buttock
Lower outer quadrant of the buttock
Upper outer quadrant of the buttock
questions.e: The sciatic nerve passes through the lower inner part of the buttock, so injections there can damage it and cause foot drop and sensory loss. The upper outer quadrant (or, preferably, the ventrogluteal site or the anterolateral thigh in children) avoids the nerve.

questions.s: A 68-year-old woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis and atrial fibrillation, not on anticoagulation, develops sudden severe pain in her right leg 3 hours ago. The leg is pale, cold and numb, and the popliteal and foot pulses are absent. The left leg pulses are normal and she has never had claudication. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sudden onset in a patient with atrial fibrillation, normal pulses in the other leg and no previous claudication points to an embolus from the left atrium. Thrombosis in situ usually occurs on a background of claudication and diseased arteries with poor collaterals forming over time.

questions.s: A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has a 4-hour history of a cold, painful left leg with absent femoral pulse but intact sensation and movement. Acute embolic ischaemia is diagnosed and theatre is being arranged. What should be given immediately?
o: Oral aspirin and review in the morning
questions.e: Immediate full anticoagulation with an intravenous heparin bolus limits propagation of thrombus beyond the embolus while embolectomy is arranged; unfractionated heparin is preferred because it can be reversed quickly in theatre. A prophylactic dose is too low to prevent propagation.

questions.s: A 65-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes has rest pain in his right foot and a non-healing toe ulcer. Foot pulses are not palpable, yet his ankle-brachial pressure index is 1.4. What best explains this ABPI?
o: Normal arterial supply to the foot
Raised blood pressure in the arm
questions.e: Medial arterial calcification in diabetes and chronic kidney disease makes the ankle arteries incompressible, giving a falsely high ABPI above about 1.3 despite significant disease. Toe pressures or duplex ultrasound are then used to assess perfusion.

questions.s: A 58-year-old man who smokes 20 cigarettes a day has cramping pain in his left calf after walking 200 metres, relieved by rest within minutes. ABPI is 0.7 on the left. He has no rest pain or tissue loss. What is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Angioplasty and stenting of the left superficial femoral artery
Smoking cessation, supervised exercise, antiplatelet and statin
questions.e: Intermittent claudication is first treated with risk factor control (stopping smoking, antiplatelet, statin, blood pressure and glucose control) and supervised exercise, which improves walking distance. Intervention is considered if symptoms remain disabling despite this, or for critical ischaemia.

questions.s: A 55-year-old male smoker complains of pain in both buttocks and thighs on walking, and erectile dysfunction for a year. Both femoral pulses are weak and the distal pulses absent. Where is the arterial disease most likely located?
questions.e: Bilateral buttock and thigh claudication with erectile dysfunction and weak femoral pulses is Leriche syndrome from aorto-iliac occlusive disease. Superficial femoral artery disease causes calf claudication with normal femoral pulses.

questions.s: A 60-year-old woman had an embolectomy for a leg ischaemic for 8 hours. Six hours after the operation her calf is tense and swollen, and she has severe pain on passive dorsiflexion of her toes, although the foot pulses are now palpable. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Elevate the leg and give stronger analgesia
Four-compartment fasciotomy of the lower leg
Duplex scan to exclude deep vein thrombosis
questions.e: Reperfusion after prolonged ischaemia causes muscle swelling within the closed fascial compartments; pain on passive stretch with a tense calf indicates compartment syndrome, which needs urgent fasciotomy. Palpable pulses do not exclude it, because compartment pressure rises above capillary pressure long before arterial flow stops.

questions.s: A 32-year-old man from Peshawar who smokes heavily has painful ulcers on his fingertips and toes, rest pain in the left foot and episodes of tender, red cords along superficial veins of his legs. He has no diabetes or high cholesterol. Which measure is most important for controlling his disease?
questions.e: Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) affects young male smokers, involving small and medium arteries and veins with migratory superficial thrombophlebitis. Complete abstinence from all tobacco, including hookah and chewed tobacco, is the only measure that halts progression and prevents amputation.

questions.s: A 66-year-old man in Islamabad has an abdominal ultrasound for renal stones. The radiologist comments on the infrarenal aorta. Above what diameter is the abdominal aorta defined as aneurysmal?
questions.e: An abdominal aorta of 3.0 cm or more in diameter is considered aneurysmal. A diameter of 5.5 cm is the usual threshold for elective repair, not for diagnosis.

questions.s: A 70-year-old man is under ultrasound surveillance for an asymptomatic infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm. He is fit for surgery. Which finding is the usual indication for elective repair?
o: Growth of 2 mm in a year
questions.e: Elective repair is usually offered for asymptomatic aneurysms of 5.5 cm or more, for rapid growth (more than about 1 cm a year), or for symptoms such as tenderness. Mural thrombus is present in most aneurysms and is not an indication by itself.

questions.s: A 74-year-old man collapses with sudden severe back and abdominal pain. He is pale and sweaty, BP 78/50 mmHg, pulse 126/min, and a tender pulsatile mass is felt above the umbilicus. A vascular surgeon is available on site. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Resuscitate with fluids to a systolic BP of 120 mmHg before deciding
Transfer to theatre without delay, accepting a low but adequate BP
Arrange urgent abdominal ultrasound to confirm the aneurysm
Admit to the ward for analgesia and observation
questions.e: An unstable patient with suspected ruptured AAA goes straight to theatre for aortic control; permissive hypotension (keeping the patient conscious with a systolic pressure of about 70-90 mmHg) limits further bleeding until the aorta is clamped. Aggressive fluid to a normal BP increases blood loss and coagulopathy, and imaging delays surgery.

questions.s: A 70-year-old man has a pulsatile swelling behind both knees. The left one is 3 cm across. What is the most common serious complication of this type of aneurysm?
o: Thrombosis or distal embolism causing acute limb ischaemia
questions.e: Popliteal aneurysms, the most common peripheral aneurysms and often bilateral, rarely rupture; their main danger is thrombosis or emboli to the tibial arteries, causing acute limb ischaemia and amputation. Rupture is the major complication of aortic aneurysms, not popliteal ones.

questions.s: A 69-year-old man is found to have an asymptomatic infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm of 4.2 cm on ultrasound. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Elective open repair within the next 3 months to prevent rupture
Regular ultrasound surveillance with risk factor control
questions.e: Aneurysms between 3.0 and 5.4 cm are managed with surveillance imaging, more often as they enlarge, together with smoking cessation and cardiovascular risk reduction. Early repair of small aneurysms has not been shown to improve survival, while operative risk is real.

questions.s: On day 2 after an open repair of an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm, a 72-year-old man passes bloody diarrhoea and develops left-sided abdominal pain, fever and a rising lactate. What is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Ligation of the inferior mesenteric artery during aneurysm repair can cause ischaemia of the left and sigmoid colon, typically presenting within days with bloody diarrhoea; sigmoidoscopy confirms it. An aorto-enteric fistula is a late complication, usually months to years after repair.

questions.s: A 55-year-old hypertensive man has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to his back. BP is 170/90 mmHg in the right arm and 130/80 mmHg in the left, and there is a new early diastolic murmur. CT angiography shows a dissection flap starting in the ascending aorta. What is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Blood pressure control alone with outpatient follow-up
questions.e: A dissection involving the ascending aorta (Stanford type A) risks rupture, tamponade, aortic regurgitation and coronary occlusion, and needs emergency surgery with blood pressure control meanwhile. Type B dissections, limited to the descending aorta, are usually managed medically. Thrombolysis is dangerous because it may be given for presumed MI.

questions.s: A house officer needs to perform an emergency venous cut-down at the ankle in a shocked patient. Which vein lies constantly just anterior to the medial malleolus?
questions.e: The great saphenous vein runs anterior to the medial malleolus, a reliable site for cut-down, and ascends the medial leg and thigh to join the femoral vein in the groin. The small saphenous vein passes behind the lateral malleolus.

questions.s: A 45-year-old schoolteacher in Lahore has bulging, aching varicose veins on the medial side of her leg and wants treatment. Which investigation should be done before planning intervention?
questions.e: Duplex ultrasound shows the sites of reflux (such as the saphenofemoral junction) and the patency of the deep veins, which determines the treatment. Venography is invasive and no longer used routinely.

questions.s: A 62-year-old woman has a shallow, painful ulcer above the medial malleolus surrounded by brown pigmentation and eczema. She has long-standing varicose veins and is a smoker. Before applying multilayer compression bandaging, which test is essential?
questions.e: Strong compression can cause pressure necrosis in a leg with arterial disease, so ABPI must be measured first; full compression is usually avoided below about 0.8. Swabs are only helpful if there are signs of infection, since all chronic ulcers are colonised.

questions.s: A 50-year-old woman with varicose veins has a soft, bluish swelling in her right groin just below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. It has a cough impulse and a palpable fluid thrill when the veins below are tapped, and disappears completely when she lies down. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A saphena varix is a dilatation of the great saphenous vein at the saphenofemoral junction: it is soft, bluish, empties on lying flat, has a cough impulse and transmits a fluid thrill on tapping the varicose veins. A femoral hernia also has a cough impulse but does not give a fluid thrill and is not usually bluish.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man has symptomatic varicose veins. Duplex shows reflux at the saphenofemoral junction and along the great saphenous vein; the deep veins are normal. Which treatment is generally recommended first for suitable patients?
o: Foam sclerotherapy of the trunk vein
questions.e: For truncal reflux in suitable patients, endovenous thermal ablation (radiofrequency or laser) is generally preferred because it has similar effectiveness with less pain and quicker recovery than open surgery. Stockings relieve symptoms but do not correct reflux.

questions.s: A 60-year-old woman with long-standing varicose veins has a lower leg that is narrow and firm just above the ankle, with brown, hardened, indurated skin, while the calf above remains full, giving an inverted champagne-bottle shape. What is this skin change called?
questions.e: Lipodermatosclerosis is fibrosis of the skin and subcutaneous fat from chronic venous hypertension, producing a hard, pigmented, contracted gaiter area and the inverted champagne-bottle leg. Lymphoedema causes swelling that includes the foot, not a narrowed ankle.

questions.s: After stripping of the great saphenous vein from the groin to the ankle, a 46-year-old woman complains of numbness and tingling along the medial side of her lower leg and foot. Which nerve has most likely been injured?
questions.e: The saphenous nerve runs with the great saphenous vein below the knee, so stripping to the ankle can damage it, causing medial leg and foot numbness; this is why stripping is usually limited to the knee. The sural nerve runs with the small saphenous vein and supplies the lateral foot.

questions.s: Saima, 34, took a 20-hour bus journey from Karachi to Islamabad and uses the combined oral contraceptive pill. She has a swollen, tender left calf, 3 cm larger than the right, with pitting oedema. Her Wells score indicates DVT is likely. What is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: When the Wells score suggests DVT is likely, a proximal leg vein ultrasound is the first-line test, ideally within 4 hours, with interim anticoagulation if delayed. A D-dimer alone cannot exclude DVT when clinical probability is high.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man has a mildly aching left calf after a long day of standing. Examination shows minimal tenderness without swelling. His Wells score indicates DVT is unlikely, and a D-dimer is negative. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Proximal leg vein ultrasound within 24 hours
No further testing for DVT; consider another diagnosis
questions.e: A negative D-dimer with a low pretest probability safely excludes DVT, so no imaging is needed and alternative causes are sought. D-dimer is sensitive but not specific: it is useful to rule out, not to rule in.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man develops a proximal DVT two weeks after a knee arthroscopy. He has no other risk factors and no previous clots. Renal and liver function are normal. For how long should he usually be anticoagulated?
questions.e: A DVT provoked by a major transient risk factor such as surgery is usually treated for 3 months, after which the risk of recurrence is low. Lifelong anticoagulation is considered for unprovoked or recurrent clots, balanced against bleeding risk.

questions.s: A 52-year-old woman with metastatic ovarian cancer has a massively swollen, painful, blue-purple left leg extending to the groin, with blisters and absent pedal pulses. Duplex shows thrombosis of the iliac and femoral veins. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Massive iliofemoral venous thrombosis can block virtually all venous outflow, raising tissue pressure until arterial inflow falls; the leg becomes swollen, blue and painful with risk of venous gangrene. Arterial embolism produces a pale, cold leg without swelling.

questions.s: A 66-year-old woman is admitted for an elective total hip replacement. She is assessed for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Which finding is a contraindication to graduated compression stockings?
o: Previous DVT in the same leg ten years ago, now fully treated
Peripheral arterial disease with an ABPI of 0.6
questions.e: Compression stockings can cause skin necrosis in limbs with arterial insufficiency, so significant peripheral arterial disease is a contraindication. Previous DVT, obesity and hormone therapy increase thrombotic risk and are reasons to give prophylaxis, not to withhold stockings.

questions.s: A 63-year-old man on prophylactic unfractionated heparin after cardiac surgery has a platelet count fall from 260 to 95 × 10^9/L on day 7, and develops a new DVT in his right leg. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Switch to low molecular weight heparin
Stop heparin and start warfarin alone immediately
Stop all heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban
questions.e: A fall in platelets of more than 50% at 5-10 days of heparin with new thrombosis suggests heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, a prothrombotic state; all heparin (including LMWH, which cross-reacts) must stop and a non-heparin anticoagulant be started. Warfarin alone at this stage can cause venous limb gangrene, and platelet transfusion may worsen thrombosis.

questions.s: Fatima, 29, is 24 weeks pregnant and has a proximal DVT of her left leg confirmed on ultrasound. What is the anticoagulant of choice for the rest of her pregnancy?
questions.e: Low molecular weight heparin does not cross the placenta and is the standard treatment for VTE in pregnancy, continued until at least 6 weeks after delivery. Warfarin is teratogenic and causes fetal bleeding, and direct oral anticoagulants are avoided in pregnancy.

questions.s: A chest drain is to be inserted in the 'safe triangle' for a large pneumothorax. Which structure forms the posterior border of this triangle?
o: Lateral border of the pectoralis major
Posterior axillary line at the 8th rib
Anterior border of the latissimus dorsi
questions.e: The safe triangle is bounded by the anterior border of latissimus dorsi posteriorly, the lateral border of pectoralis major anteriorly, and a line at the level of the nipple (5th intercostal space) inferiorly, with the apex below the axilla. Inserting below the nipple line risks injury to the diaphragm, liver or spleen.

questions.s: A trainee is inserting a chest drain in the 5th intercostal space. Why should the dissection pass immediately over the upper border of the rib below?
o: To avoid the long thoracic nerve
To avoid the intercostal neurovascular bundle
To place the tube closer to the apex of the lung
To avoid the internal thoracic artery
questions.e: The intercostal vein, artery and nerve run in the costal groove along the lower border of each rib, so passing just above the rib below avoids them. The internal thoracic artery runs near the sternal edge, well away from the safe triangle.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man has a large malignant pleural effusion drained through a chest drain. About 3 litres drain within 30 minutes. He then develops a persistent cough, breathlessness and hypoxia, and the radiograph shows new air-space shadowing in the drained lung only. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Rapid drainage of a large effusion or pneumothorax that has been present for some time can cause unilateral re-expansion pulmonary oedema; drainage of large effusions is therefore done in stages with the drain clamped intermittently. Cardiogenic oedema would usually be bilateral.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man with a chest drain for a traumatic haemopneumothorax becomes more breathless. The fluid in the drain tubing no longer rises and falls with respiration, nothing is draining, and breath sounds on that side are reduced. What is the most likely cause?
o: Normal drain function in a resolving pneumothorax
The underwater seal bottle is too low
The drain is blocked, kinked or displaced
questions.e: Loss of swing with worsening breathlessness and reduced breath sounds means the drain is no longer in communication with the pleural space because it is blocked, kinked or displaced; it should be checked and imaged. Absent swing from full lung re-expansion would come with clinical improvement, not deterioration.

questions.s: A 28-year-old man with a chest drain for a spontaneous pneumothorax is being moved to a ward. The drain is bubbling continuously. The porter asks whether to clamp the tube for the journey. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Clamp the tube until he reaches the ward
Do not clamp it, and keep the bottle below chest level
Disconnect the bottle and seal the end of the tube with a sterile spigot
Lay the bottle on its side on the bed
questions.e: Clamping a bubbling drain traps air in the pleural space and can cause tension pneumothorax; the bottle should stay upright and below the level of the chest so that fluid cannot siphon back. Laying the bottle on its side may break the underwater seal.

questions.s: A day after a chest drain is inserted for a pneumothorax, a 40-year-old man develops increasing swelling and crackling under the skin around the drain site, spreading to the neck. The radiograph shows the most proximal side hole of the drain lying outside the rib cage. What is the most likely cause of the surgical emphysema?
o: Infection of the drain site with gas-forming bacteria such as clostridia
Partial withdrawal of the drain with a side hole in the chest wall
Normal finding after any chest drain insertion
Rupture of the oesophagus during insertion
questions.e: If the drain slips out so that a side hole lies in the chest wall, air from the pleural space escapes into the soft tissues, causing spreading surgical emphysema; the drain needs to be repositioned or replaced. Gas gangrene is far rarer and would cause systemic toxicity and wound changes.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man treated for 5 days for right lower lobe pneumonia is still febrile. Ultrasound shows a moderate pleural effusion. Diagnostic aspiration yields cloudy but not purulent fluid with pH 7.05 and low glucose. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Continue the same antibiotics and repeat the radiograph in 2 weeks
Change to oral antibiotics and discharge
questions.e: A parapneumonic effusion with a pleural fluid pH below 7.2 (or frank pus, or organisms on Gram stain) is a complicated effusion or empyema that will not resolve with antibiotics alone and needs chest drainage. Repeated aspiration leaves infected fluid behind.

questions.s: A 48-year-old diabetic man has fever and right pleuritic chest pain 2 weeks after pneumonia. Ultrasound-guided aspiration of a right pleural effusion yields thick, foul-smelling pus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Frank pus in the pleural space is an empyema, which needs drainage and prolonged antibiotics; a foul smell suggests anaerobes. A chylothorax gives milky fluid rich in triglycerides, not foul pus.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man has had a right empyema for 6 weeks despite antibiotics and a chest drain. He is still febrile. CT shows a thick pleural rind encasing the lung, which cannot expand. He is fit for surgery. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: In the organising stage, a fibrous peel traps the lung; surgical decortication removes the peel and allows the lung to re-expand, controlling sepsis. Further drains cannot remove a solid peel, and pleurodesis is used for recurrent malignant effusion or pneumothorax, not infection.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man from rural Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has 6 weeks of low-grade fever, night sweats, weight loss and a right pleural effusion. Pleural fluid is a straw-coloured exudate with predominantly lymphocytes and a high adenosine deaminase. Gram stain is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A lymphocyte-rich exudate with high adenosine deaminase in a young person with constitutional symptoms in a high-burden country strongly suggests tuberculous pleurisy; pleural biopsy can confirm granulomas. Parapneumonic effusions are neutrophil-predominant.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man with an untreated chronic empyema develops a fluctuant, tender swelling on his chest wall overlying the affected side. When pressed, it decreases in size and he coughs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Empyema necessitans is the spread of pus from the pleural space through the chest wall into the subcutaneous tissue, forming a fluctuant mass that communicates with the pleura; tuberculosis and actinomycosis are classic causes. A lipoma is soft, painless and does not communicate with the pleural cavity.

questions.s: A 78-year-old woman with severe COPD has a multiloculated empyema. Despite a correctly placed chest drain and antibiotics, the collection persists and she remains septic. The surgeons consider her unfit for surgery. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Intrapleural tissue plasminogen activator with DNase
Remove the drain and continue oral antibiotics
questions.e: Intrapleural fibrinolytic (tPA) combined with DNase breaks down loculations and improves drainage in patients with pleural infection who fail drainage and are not fit for surgery. Talc pleurodesis is contraindicated in active pleural infection.

questions.s: A 70-year-old diabetic smoker has burning pain in his right foot at night that wakes him from sleep; he gets relief by hanging the leg over the side of the bed. The foot is pale on elevation and dusky red when dependent. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Ischaemic rest pain relieved by dependency, with pallor on elevation and dependent rubor, indicates critical limb ischaemia, which threatens the limb and needs urgent vascular referral. Intermittent claudication occurs only on walking and settles with rest.

questions.s: A 65-year-old man with disabling claudication despite exercise and medical therapy is being considered for revascularisation. Which imaging is usually done first to define the arterial disease?
questions.e: Duplex ultrasound is the first-line, non-invasive imaging to locate and grade stenoses, followed by CT or MR angiography if more detail is needed for planning. Digital subtraction angiography is invasive and is now mainly used during endovascular treatment.

questions.s: Two days after a coronary angiogram through the right femoral artery, a 58-year-old man has a painful, pulsatile swelling in his right groin with a systolic bruit. Distal pulses are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A pulsatile groin mass with a bruit after arterial puncture is a false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm), a contained leak through the puncture site; duplex confirms it and many are treated with ultrasound-guided thrombin injection. An abscess is not pulsatile and causes fever and redness.

questions.s: A 67-year-old man with a 4.6 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm under surveillance asks what he can do to reduce the chance of it growing. Which modifiable factor is most strongly associated with faster growth and rupture?
questions.e: Continued smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for aneurysm formation, growth and rupture, so stopping smoking is the key advice. Blood pressure control and statin therapy reduce overall cardiovascular risk as well.

questions.s: In a patient with varicose veins, the leg is elevated to empty the veins and a tourniquet is placed around the upper thigh. On standing, the veins stay empty until the tourniquet is released, when they fill rapidly from above. What does this indicate?
questions.e: Rapid filling from above only after the tourniquet is released, with the veins controlled while it is in place, localises reflux to the saphenofemoral junction (a positive tourniquet test). Filling despite the tourniquet would suggest incompetent perforators or reflux lower down. Duplex has largely replaced these bedside tests.

questions.s: A 50-year-old woman with varicose veins has a painful, red, tender cord along the great saphenous vein extending to the upper thigh, within about 3 cm of the groin crease. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Oral antibiotics and review in 1 week
Urgent duplex ultrasound to assess the saphenofemoral junction and deep veins
Immediate surgical excision of the whole thrombosed segment of vein
questions.e: Superficial thrombophlebitis extending close to the saphenofemoral junction can propagate into the deep venous system, and a coexisting DVT is common, so duplex is needed to guide anticoagulation. It is an inflammatory thrombosis, not an infection, so antibiotics are not indicated.

questions.s: A 60-year-old woman is immobile for several days after an abdominal hysterectomy. In which veins do most postoperative deep vein thromboses begin?
questions.e: Most postoperative DVTs start in the soleal sinuses and deep calf veins, where flow is slowest during immobility, and some then extend proximally. The great saphenous vein is superficial; thrombosis there is superficial thrombophlebitis.

questions.s: A 58-year-old man has an acute proximal femoral DVT. Ten days ago he had a haemorrhagic stroke, and the neurologists advise that anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated for now. What is the most appropriate way to reduce his risk of pulmonary embolism?
questions.e: An inferior vena cava filter is indicated for proximal DVT when anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated, as after recent intracranial haemorrhage; anticoagulation is started and the filter removed once it becomes safe. Thrombolysis carries even greater bleeding risk than anticoagulation.

questions.s: A 24-year-old man needs a chest drain for a large traumatic pneumothorax. At which site is the drain usually inserted?
o: 5th intercostal space, just anterior to the mid-axillary line
questions.e: Chest drains are placed in the safe triangle, usually in the 4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line, which avoids the great vessels, breast tissue and the diaphragm. Low posterior sites risk injury to the liver or spleen.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man has a pleural effusion. Pleural fluid protein is 38 g/L with serum protein 64 g/L; pleural LDH is 150 IU/L with serum LDH 300 IU/L (upper limit 250). How is the effusion classified by Light's criteria?
o: Transudate, because the LDH ratio is 0.5
Transudate, because pleural LDH is below the serum upper limit
Exudate, because the protein ratio exceeds 0.5
It cannot be classified without pleural glucose
questions.e: Light's criteria define an exudate if any one criterion is met: pleural/serum protein ratio above 0.5, pleural/serum LDH ratio above 0.6, or pleural LDH above two-thirds of the serum upper limit. The protein ratio here is about 0.59, so it is an exudate even though the LDH criteria are not met.

questions.s: A 2-year-old boy from rural Sindh is admitted with severe pneumonia after measles. The chest radiograph shows thin-walled air cysts (pneumatoceles) and a pleural effusion; aspiration yields pus. Which organism is most likely?
questions.e: Pneumatoceles with empyema in a young child, particularly after measles or influenza, are characteristic of Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia, which needs an anti-staphylococcal antibiotic and drainage. Mycoplasma and RSV rarely cause empyema.

questions.s: A 62-year-old woman treated for community-acquired pneumonia has persistent fever and a rising CRP after 4 days of antibiotics. Chest radiograph shows a new blunting of the right costophrenic angle, and ultrasound shows a moderate effusion with some septations. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Change antibiotics and repeat the radiograph in a week
questions.e: An effusion with persistent sepsis during pneumonia must be sampled to look for pleural infection; pH, Gram stain and culture decide whether a chest drain is needed. Changing antibiotics alone leaves a possible empyema undrained.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man has a slowly growing frontal meningioma. For many months his intracranial pressure stays normal despite the enlarging mass, and then it rises steeply over a few days. In the early compensated phase, which mechanism mainly keeps the pressure normal?
o: Displacement of CSF and venous blood
Increased CSF production by the choroid plexus
Expansion of the skull at the sutures
Rise in cerebral arterial blood volume
questions.e: By the Monro-Kellie doctrine the skull is a fixed box, so an expanding mass is first accommodated by pushing CSF into the spinal theca and squeezing venous blood out; once these reserves are used up, small increases in volume cause steep rises in pressure. CSF production does not increase, and adult sutures are fused.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man with a severe head injury is ventilated in the ICU in Lahore. His mean arterial pressure is 80 mmHg, and an intracranial pressure monitor reads 25 mmHg. What is his cerebral perfusion pressure?
questions.e: Cerebral perfusion pressure equals mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure: 80 − 25 = 55 mmHg. This is below the usual target of about 60-70 mmHg, so treatment aims both to lower ICP and to maintain blood pressure.

questions.s: A 45-year-old woman has had headaches for 6 weeks that are worst on waking and with coughing, with early-morning vomiting. Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilloedema, and there is mild left-sided weakness. Which procedure should be avoided until brain imaging has been done?
questions.e: Morning headache, vomiting, papilloedema and a focal deficit suggest a space-occupying lesion with raised intracranial pressure. Lumbar puncture in this setting can cause a pressure gradient and herniation of the brain, so imaging must come first.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman with a posterior fossa tumour and hydrocephalus complains of double vision when looking to the right. Her right eye cannot move outwards beyond the midline. There is no lesion near the brainstem nucleus on MRI. Which cranial nerve is affected?
questions.e: The abducens nerve has a long intracranial course over the petrous apex and is easily stretched when pressure rises, causing a lateral rectus palsy that is a false localising sign. The oculomotor nerve is compressed by uncal herniation, producing a dilated pupil and ptosis rather than failure of abduction.

questions.s: A 7-year-old boy with a midline cerebellar tumour has had morning vomiting and unsteadiness for a month. Today he becomes drowsy (GCS 11). CT shows the tumour obstructing the fourth ventricle with markedly dilated lateral and third ventricles. What is the most appropriate immediate procedure?
questions.e: Acute obstructive hydrocephalus with falling consciousness needs urgent CSF diversion, and an external ventricular drain relieves pressure above the block quickly. A lumbar drain is dangerous in obstructive hydrocephalus because it lowers pressure below the obstruction and can cause tonsillar herniation; steroids alone act too slowly.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man with a large intracerebral haemorrhage is awaiting neurosurgical transfer. His GCS falls from 12 to 8 and his right pupil begins to enlarge. He is intubated. Which immediate measure will lower his intracranial pressure while surgery is arranged?
questions.e: An osmotic agent such as mannitol (or hypertonic saline) draws water out of the brain and lowers ICP as a bridge to surgery; the head is kept up at about 30° to aid venous drainage. Hypotonic fluids such as 5% dextrose worsen cerebral oedema, and a high PaCO2 dilates cerebral vessels and raises ICP.

questions.s: A 60-year-old woman with lung cancer has headaches and mild right-sided weakness. MRI shows a single brain metastasis surrounded by extensive white-matter oedema. Which drug will most quickly reduce the oedema and her symptoms?
questions.e: Vasogenic oedema around brain tumours and metastases responds well to corticosteroids such as dexamethasone, which reduce leakiness of the blood-brain barrier. Steroids do not help, and may harm, in traumatic brain injury; nimodipine is used to prevent vasospasm after subarachnoid haemorrhage.

questions.s: A 4-month-old baby has a head circumference rising across centiles, a tense bulging anterior fontanelle, distended scalp veins and eyes that are deviated downwards. Which investigation is most appropriate first?
questions.e: The signs suggest infantile hydrocephalus, and while the anterior fontanelle is open, cranial ultrasound shows ventricular size quickly without radiation or sedation. Lumbar puncture is dangerous if the hydrocephalus is obstructive, and a skull X-ray does not show the ventricles.

questions.s: A 20-year-old man is hit on the side of the head with a cricket ball. CT shows a fracture of the squamous temporal bone in the region of the pterion with a biconvex haematoma beneath it. Which vessel has most likely bled?
questions.e: The middle meningeal artery runs deep to the pterion, where the skull is thin, so a fracture here tears it and produces an extradural haematoma. Bridging veins cause subdural haematomas, which are crescent-shaped rather than biconvex.

questions.s: A CT scan is reviewed in a neurosurgical meeting for a patient who had a head injury. Which CT appearance is typical of an acute extradural haematoma?
o: Blood in the basal cisterns and sulci
questions.e: In an extradural haematoma blood strips the dura from the skull, but the dura is firmly attached at the sutures, so the clot forms a lens shape that does not cross suture lines. A crescentic collection crossing sutures is subdural, and blood in the cisterns is subarachnoid.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man has an acute temporal extradural haematoma of about 40 mL with 7 mm midline shift after a fall from a roof. His GCS has fallen from 14 to 11 over an hour. A neurosurgeon is available on site. What is the most appropriate management?
o: IV mannitol and observation in HDU
Conservative care with repeat CT in 6 hours
questions.e: An extradural haematoma over about 30 mL, with midline shift and falling GCS, needs urgent craniotomy and evacuation; outcomes are excellent when it is done before the brain is irreversibly compressed. Mannitol is only a bridge, and lumbar puncture risks herniation.

questions.s: A 78-year-old woman on aspirin has 3 weeks of increasing confusion and mild right-sided weakness after a minor fall. CT shows a left-sided crescentic collection that is hypodense compared with brain, with 8 mm midline shift and no acute blood. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Observation and repeat CT in 4 weeks
questions.e: A symptomatic chronic subdural haematoma has liquefied, so it can be drained through burr holes, usually with a drain left in to reduce recurrence. Observation is only for small asymptomatic collections, and a large craniotomy is unnecessary for liquid haematoma.

questions.s: A surgical trainee asks why chronic subdural haematomas are much more common in elderly people and in people with long-standing alcohol misuse, often after only trivial head injury. What is the best explanation?
o: Thin skull bones fracture more easily
Reduced CSF production around the brain
questions.e: Cerebral atrophy enlarges the space between brain and dura, so the bridging veins crossing it are stretched and tear with minor acceleration forces, bleeding slowly into the subdural space. Hypertensive perforator rupture causes intracerebral, not subdural, haemorrhage.

questions.s: A 5-month-old baby is brought with seizures and irritability. The parents report no injury. CT shows bilateral subdural haematomas of different ages, and fundoscopy shows extensive retinal haemorrhages. Clotting studies are normal, and he received vitamin K at birth. What is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Subdural haematomas of different ages with retinal haemorrhages and no plausible history in an infant strongly suggest abusive head trauma from shaking; safeguarding procedures must be started. Normal clotting and vitamin K at birth argue against bleeding disorders, and birth-related bleeds would have resolved by 5 months.

questions.s: After a road accident, a 28-year-old man opens his eyes only to a painful stimulus, says random words that do not make sense in the conversation, and reaches up to push the examiner's hand away from his supraorbital ridge. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale score?
questions.e: Eye opening to pain scores 2, inappropriate words score 3 and localising to pain scores 5, giving a GCS of 10. Confused but sentence-forming speech would score 4, and incomprehensible sounds would score 2.

questions.s: Two young men are admitted after head injuries, one with an acute extradural and one with an acute subdural haematoma of similar volume, both evacuated within 2 hours. The registrar explains that the patient with the subdural haematoma has a worse expected outcome. What is the main reason?
questions.e: Acute subdural haematoma usually results from high-energy injury with tearing of cortical vessels and is accompanied by contusion and diffuse injury to the underlying brain, which determines the poor outcome. In extradural haematoma the brain is often relatively uninjured, so prompt evacuation gives excellent recovery.

questions.s: A 10-year-old girl is listed for excision of a midline neck cyst just below the hyoid that moves upwards on tongue protrusion. The surgeon explains that, to reduce the risk of recurrence, the operation will also remove a related structure. Which structure is removed with the cyst?
o: Central part of the hyoid bone
questions.e: The thyroglossal tract passes through or close to the body of the hyoid, so Sistrunk's operation removes the cyst, the tract and the central part of the hyoid up towards the foramen caecum. Simple cyst excision leaves tract remnants and has a high recurrence rate.

questions.s: A 22-year-old woman from Quetta has had painless swellings on the left side of her neck for 3 months. The nodes in the posterior triangle are matted together, and one has become soft and fluctuant without redness or warmth. She has low-grade evening fever. Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Matted nodes with a cold abscess suggest tuberculous lymphadenitis, and fine-needle aspiration for cytology, acid-fast bacilli and Xpert MTB/RIF confirms it and detects rifampicin resistance. A tuberculin test cannot distinguish active from latent infection, and a normal chest X-ray does not exclude nodal TB.

questions.s: A 58-year-old man who has smoked for 40 years has a 3 cm hard, painless lump at the angle of the jaw, present for 6 weeks. He has mild hoarseness. There is no sign of infection. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: Open excision biopsy of the node
Two weeks of antibiotics and review
questions.e: A hard, persistent neck node in an older smoker is metastatic squamous cell carcinoma until proven otherwise, and ultrasound-guided FNA is the first test, followed by examination of the upper aerodigestive tract to find the primary. Open biopsy before the primary is found can seed tumour and compromise later neck dissection.

questions.s: A 45-year-old woman has a slowly growing, painless lump at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, deep to the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid. It is pulsatile, can be moved from side to side but not up and down, and imaging shows it splaying the internal and external carotid arteries. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A paraganglioma at the carotid bifurcation transmits pulsation, moves sideways but not vertically, and splays the internal and external carotids on imaging. Biopsy should be avoided because it is highly vascular; an aneurysm is expansile and does not splay the bifurcation.

questions.s: A 24-year-old man has several rubbery, painless lymph nodes in the left supraclavicular region and lower neck, enlarging over 2 months. He has drenching night sweats, itching, and the nodes ache after drinking alcohol. Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Suspected lymphoma (here Hodgkin lymphoma, with B symptoms and alcohol-induced pain) needs excision or core biopsy of a whole node so the architecture can be assessed for classification. FNA cytology is inadequate for diagnosing and typing lymphoma.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman had a lymph node removed from the posterior triangle of the neck. Afterwards she has an aching shoulder, cannot shrug it fully, and has difficulty raising her arm above her head. Which nerve has been injured?
questions.e: The spinal accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle superficially and supplies trapezius, so injury causes shoulder drooping, weak shrug and difficulty abducting above 90°. The great auricular nerve is sensory to the ear lobe and angle of the jaw.

questions.s: A 15-year-old boy has had intermittent mucoid discharge from a small opening at the anterior border of the lower third of sternocleidomastoid since childhood. A fistulogram shows the tract passing upwards between the internal and external carotid arteries. Where is its internal opening most likely to be?
questions.e: A second branchial cleft fistula runs from the lower anterior border of sternocleidomastoid, between the internal and external carotid arteries, to open into the tonsillar fossa. Third and fourth arch remnants open into the pyriform fossa, and the foramen caecum is the origin of the thyroglossal tract.

questions.s: A 6-week-old baby born by difficult breech delivery holds her head tilted to the right with the chin turned to the left. There is a firm, painless, 2 cm mass within the right sternocleidomastoid muscle. Ultrasound confirms a fibrous swelling within the muscle. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: A sternomastoid tumour (fibromatosis colli) causing congenital torticollis usually resolves with passive stretching exercises taught to the parents. Surgery to release the muscle is reserved for persistent torticollis after about a year of physiotherapy.

questions.s: A 45-year-old woman has a slowly growing, painless, 3 cm mass in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland. FNA cytology shows a pleomorphic adenoma, and facial nerve function is normal. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Pleomorphic adenoma has finger-like extensions through an incomplete capsule, so it is removed with a cuff of normal tissue by superficial parotidectomy, preserving the facial nerve. Enucleation leaves microscopic tumour behind and leads to multifocal recurrence.

questions.s: Eight months after a superficial parotidectomy, a 50-year-old man notices that the skin in front of his left ear becomes red and sweaty whenever he eats. Aberrant regeneration of fibres from which nerve explains this?
questions.e: In Frey's syndrome, parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the parotid, carried in the auriculotemporal nerve, regrow into the cut sympathetic supply of the skin's sweat glands, so eating causes gustatory sweating and flushing. The great auricular nerve is often divided at parotidectomy, but it causes numbness of the ear lobe instead.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man has a hard, fixed lump in the left parotid region that has grown over 4 months and is now painful. He has weakness of the left side of his face, including the forehead. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.e: Facial nerve palsy with a hard, fixed, painful parotid mass strongly suggests malignancy, and mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the commonest malignant parotid tumour. Benign tumours such as pleomorphic adenoma and Warthin's tumour almost never cause facial weakness.

questions.s: A 52-year-old woman has a slow-growing submucosal swelling of the hard palate and numbness over the upper lip and cheek on the same side. Biopsy shows small basaloid cells arranged in a cribriform, Swiss-cheese pattern, with tumour surrounding nerve bundles. What is the diagnosis?
questions.e: Adenoid cystic carcinoma, common in minor salivary glands of the palate, has a cribriform pattern and characteristically spreads along nerves, causing numbness or pain. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma contains mucous and squamoid cells without this marked perineural tendency.

questions.s: A 76-year-old man is dehydrated after an emergency laparotomy and has poor oral hygiene. On day 4 he develops a painful, red, swollen right parotid region with fever, and pus can be expressed from the parotid duct opening. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.e: Acute suppurative parotitis in a dehydrated, postoperative patient with reduced salivary flow is usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus ascending the duct. Mumps causes non-suppurative, often bilateral swelling, and pus would not be expressed from the duct.

questions.s: A 15-year-old boy from a village near Sukkur has bilateral painful swelling in front of both ears and fever. He was not vaccinated. Five days later he develops a painful, swollen right testis. What is the most likely cause of the testicular swelling?
questions.e: Orchitis is a common complication of mumps after puberty, typically appearing a few days after the parotitis. Torsion causes sudden severe pain without preceding parotitis, and Chlamydia is a sexually transmitted cause unlikely in this setting.

questions.s: After excision of the left submandibular gland for recurrent stones, a 45-year-old man notices that the left corner of his lower lip does not move down when he smiles. Which nerve has been injured?
o: Buccal branch of the facial nerve
questions.e: The marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve runs just below the mandible over the submandibular gland and supplies depressor anguli oris, so the incision is placed well below the jaw to protect it. Lingual nerve injury causes tongue numbness, and hypoglossal injury causes tongue deviation.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man has a stone in Wharton's duct confirmed on imaging. He asks why most salivary stones form in the submandibular gland rather than the parotid. What is the best explanation?
o: Larger size of the submandibular gland
Viscous, alkaline saliva and an uphill duct
Higher bacterial load in the floor of the mouth
Absence of myoepithelial cells in the gland
questions.e: Submandibular saliva is more mucous, more alkaline and richer in calcium, and the duct runs upwards against gravity, which favours stasis and precipitation. Parotid saliva is watery and serous, so stones are less common there.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man who has used naswar (snuff) placed in his mouth for 25 years has a white patch on the inner lower lip that cannot be wiped off. It has been present for 3 months and is painless. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.e: A persistent white patch that cannot be wiped off is leukoplakia, a potentially malignant disorder, and biopsy is needed to look for dysplasia or carcinoma. Candida plaques wipe off, and destroying the lesion without histology could miss cancer.

questions.s: A dental surgeon screening tobacco users at a rural health centre in Punjab finds several types of oral mucosal lesions. Which lesion carries the highest risk of malignant transformation?
